title: The Windows XP Trap: How "Good Enough" Artificial Intelligence Could Strand the Most Expensive Capital Stock in History — and Why Arriving Late May Yet Become Europe's Advantage
affiliations: University of La Laguna

detail.title: The Windows XP Trap: How "Good Enough" Artificial Intelligence Could Strand the Most Expensive Capital Stock in History — and Why Arriving Late May Yet Become Europe's Advantage

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. The author has no personal or financial relationship with any of the companies, institutions or public bodies discussed in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no specific funding from any agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
This paper makes a forecast. The decisive economic threshold of the artificial-intelligence era will not be the arrival of superintelligence but the arrival of sufficiency: the point at which inexpensive, open-weight or locally deployable models can satisfy almost everything that most people and firms actually demand of them. Recent evidence on AI use shows that demand remains concentrated in practical guidance, information seeking, writing, learning and other bounded, readily verifiable tasks. If cheap models cross the sufficiency threshold, the frontier can keep advancing while the mass market stops paying to follow it.

The forecast has a second half. The historic AI infrastructure build-out now under way - including roughly a trillion dollars of data-centre lease commitments that have not yet commenced, nearly four times the lease liabilities already recognised - is being contracted at scarcity-phase prices while financing the technological and organisational learning that makes each subsequent generation of equivalent capacity cheaper. If sufficiency arrives while material scarcity-priced cohorts still depend on future rents to complete their investment case, falling willingness to pay and falling replacement cost can compress their expected returns even where the installed capacity remains operationally competitive. The resulting losses need not appear as the failure of the famous technology companies. They can surface first in the financing chain behind the build-out: lessors, special-purpose vehicles, specialised compute providers and their creditors, through lower utilisation, compressed returns, impairments and renegotiated commitments.

The conjunction of demand-side sufficiency and a capital-vintage penalty, written S_p > 1 and V > 1, identifies the regime in which late entry becomes possible; a late-mover arbitrage arises only where fresh capital also undercuts the incumbent's economically relevant defensive cost: an entrant no longer needs the best AI, only sufficient AI produced more cheaply. Applied to the European Union, this yields a conditional second chance. Europe's relatively younger future capital stock is an advantage only if it can mobilise capital, narrow its energy-cost disadvantage, preserve technological exit options and maintain the political capacity to act. The paper derives eleven measurable forecasts and states explicit conditions under which its central hypothesis would be falsified. A Spanish-language version of this paper is available from the author.

title: AI-generated Summaries in Prediction Markets
affiliations: University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration, University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration,  and University of Florida - Warrington College of Business Administration

detail.title: AI-generated Summaries in Prediction Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Prediction markets rely on diverse participants' informational inputs to aggregate dispersed information into accurate collective forecasts. To reduce barriers to market participation, leading prediction market platforms have recently begun integrating AI-generated summaries (AIGS) that synthesize contextual information and market-relevant news. Because information is critical to the functioning of prediction markets, the emergence of AIGS as a new channel for delivering market-relevant information may reshape both how users access and process information and how markets aggregate dispersed information. Yet, despite the growing adoption of AIGS, little is known about its broader implications for prediction markets. To address this gap, we leverage Polymarket's introduction of AIGS to examine its impact on individual trading behavior and market forecasting performance. We find that AIGS significantly increases individual participation and makes users more likely to trade in the direction suggested by AIGS. These behavioral changes characterize what we refer to as the AI herding effect: exposure to AI-generated summaries increases individuals' tendency to rely on them when forming judgments and making decisions. Our laboratory experiment provides further evidence for this effect and sheds light on its underlying mechanism, showing that AIGS increases trading participation by reducing information acquisition and processing costs while shifting participants' beliefs toward the direction conveyed by the AIGS. At the market level, we find that AIGS reduces prediction accuracy and market efficiency. Taken together, these findings suggest that the introduction of AIGS presents a double-edged sword: while it makes prediction markets more accessible, it may unexpectedly harm the core function of prediction markets by undermining collective information aggregation. These findings contribute to the emerging literature on generative AI and collective intelligence by revealing how AI-generated information can affect information aggregation on digital platforms.

title: Your AI May Learn What Your Company Rewards, Not What Works
affiliations: University of Auckland School of Business

detail.title: Your AI May Learn What Your Company Rewards, Not What Works

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.ethicsApproval: None required.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract: As firms increasingly use proprietary enterprise data to train and evaluate AI, a less obvious problem emerges: organisational archives often record what was approved, rewarded and repeated more clearly than whether the underlying decisions were sound. Using the proposed sale of Spirit Airlines' internal data as an illustrative case, this paper develops the idea of an approval-performance gap between observable organisational signals and the quality of the judgement they represent. It argues that enterprise AI may reproduce historical incentives, biases and assumptions if organisational records are treated simply as demonstrations of successful behaviour. The paper proposes decision provenance as a way of preserving the information, assumptions, alternatives and outcomes surrounding consequential decisions, and suggests using reconstructed historical decisions as blind evaluation cases before they are used for AI training. This approach turns organisational history from material to imitate into an organisation-specific environment for testing both machine and managerial judgement.

detail.abstract: Verification as currently taught asks whether a case is good law. Attorneys need to know whether a proposition is usable: still valid, governing in the relevant forum and procedural posture, helpful to the represented party, and not already rejected in the jurisdiction. Each concept exists somewhere in research competencies or commercial tools, but they remain dispersed, never unified into a proposition-level verification protocol for AI-assisted legal research. This article proposes that unification as a proposition-usability model, assesses how far Shepard’s, KeyCite, and Westlaw Precision already reach, and offers a classroom exercise and vendor-evaluation questions law librarians can apply now.

title: Impact of Last-Mile Delivery Costs on Financial Stability: A Comparative Study of Quick Commerce and E-commerce in India
affiliations: PES University and Symbiosis Institute of Business Management, Nagpur

detail.title: Impact of Last-Mile Delivery Costs on Financial Stability: A Comparative Study of Quick Commerce and E-commerce in India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The Research was self funded

detail.abstract:
The present study is focused on the effect of last-mile delivery costs on the financial sustainability of the e-commerce and quick-commerce companies operating in India. Amazon Seller Services Pvt. Ltd. has been considered as the e-commerce benchmark company whereas Swiggy Ltd., along with its Instamart quick-commerce division, has been taken as the quickcommerce benchmark company. Using five-year standardized financial statement data (CMIE Prowess) of both the firms, this research has employed the techniques of ratio analysis, trend analysis, common-size analysis, and correlation analysis with the Selling & Distribution Expense acting as a proxy for last-mile delivery cost due to lack of specific reporting. 

These results indicate that the delivery-cost intensity of both firms is highly negatively correlated with net profit margin (-0.96 for Amazon and-0.76 for Swiggy) and that both firms have decreased delivery-cost intensity as a proportion of revenue during the period of study. Yet, better delivery-cost efficiency does not necessarily imply greater stability from a financial point of view. Amazon managed to turn its efficiency into self-sustained positive operating cash flow, whereas Swiggy remained financing-dependent over the entire period despite making greater progress in terms of contribution margin. Traditional measures of liquidity were deceptive in this case, since Swiggy had higher current ratio than Amazon but was still financed liquidity driven. 

This paper finds that the financial stability of digital commerce is more driven by factors like the level of development of the network, the existence of costs other than delivery costs such as customer acquisition costs, and market access rather than the cost efficiency of delivery only. The paper provides a delivery-cost-based margin structure and demonstrates the weaknesses of using static liquidity ratios.

title: Ethical AI in Practice
affiliations: The Digital Economist

detail.title: Ethical AI in Practice

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no financial, personal, or professional relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Ethical AI in Practice: Governance Strategies for Responsible and Accountable AI Deployment examines the widening gap between rapid AI adoption and the slower development of governance mechanisms across institutions. As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in decision-making processes across healthcare, finance, employment, and public administration, the paper argues that the core challenge is no longer technological capability, but the ability of institutions to govern these systems effectively.

The paper analyzes key risks—including bias, opacity, uneven institutional capacity, and operational failures—demonstrating how governance gaps translate into real-world consequences. Drawing on emerging research and comparative policy approaches, it highlights the limitations of fragmented oversight and emphasizes the need for structured, lifecycle-based governance models that integrate risk classification, data governance, validation, human oversight, and continuous monitoring.

Moving from diagnosis to implementation, the paper proposes a practical governance framework supported by a readiness assessment tool to help institutions operationalize ethical principles at scale. It concludes with targeted policy recommendations, calling for coordinated action to embed governance into system design, strengthen institutional capacity, and align oversight with the pace of technological advancement.

title: The Resolution Paradox: How Optimizing for AI Visibility Reduces the Need for Brand Contact — and What Firms Can Do About It

detail.title: The Resolution Paradox: How Optimizing for AI Visibility Reduces the Need for Brand Contact — and What Firms Can Do About It

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received to assist with the preparation of this manuscript.

detail.abstract: Generative AI systems increasingly enable users to complete more of their goals within the interaction itself rather than through referral to external sources. Firms respond by optimizing content for AI visibility, treating success at the level of the answer — utilization and citation — as sufficient. We argue that answer-level success is not the same as business-level consequence. The same content property that makes a firm’s brand information useful to a generative system — its resolvability, that is, its capacity to enable the system to fulfill a given type of user goal — raises the probability of utilization; realized utilization, in turn, contributes to AI-mediated goal completion, reducing the user’s functional need to interact with the brand directly. We refer to the resulting asymmetry as the resolution paradox: the reduction in functional need follows from the goal completion enabled by successful utilization, whereas a second effect — strengthened preference toward the brand — depends on favorable perceivable brand attribution, a separate state of the AI answer that may correlate with utilization but is neither determined by it nor guaranteed by the brand. Integrating research on generative engine optimization, zero-click search, disintermediation, decision support systems, and relationship marketing, we develop a two-chain model in which utilization initiates a functional disintermediation pathway, while attribution opens a distinct motivational preference pathway. In short, the cost is tied to being used; the compensation depends on being named favorably — and the two do not reliably coincide. Firms cannot avoid the paradox simply by degrading or withholding substitutable public content, but they can compensate for it through residual-value assets that retain independent value despite increasing AI-mediated goal completion. The model explains why comparable AI-mediated resolution can produce divergent economic consequences across actors and yields falsifiable propositions and a research agenda for AI-mediated brand interaction. At the ecosystem level, the mechanism implies a redistribution of value according to what remains functionally and motivationally valuable for different actors, shifting the basis of competitive advantage beyond visibility toward the capabilities and relationships that remain valuable as AI resolves more of users’ goals.

title: Privacy, Power, and the Boardroom: Constitutionalising Corporate Governance Under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

detail.title: Privacy, Power, and the Boardroom: Constitutionalising Corporate Governance Under India’s Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 of India reflects a major change in the manner in which organisations approach the management of personal data. The Act views privacy as a matter of governance that requires boardroom attention and integration into corporate governance structures. The DPDP Act substantiates the rights-based approach through the specification of the fiduciary duties of corporate boards. To be precise, the approach is underpinned by the Supreme Court’s ruling that the right to privacy is a fundamental right, as held in the judgment in the case of Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India (2017). The current study argues that the DPDP Act successfully embeds data governance in the Constitution, requiring boards to act in the best interests of data principals, thereby moving the focus from compliance to a duty of care. This article illustrates that the management of personal data has become an essential part of risk management, internal controls, and corporate responsibility, and it includes concepts of Indian company law, the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and current judicial expectations regarding digital accountability. It also includes a comparative analysis of the EU’s GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 of the United Kingdom. Essentially, the current paper encourages the reconsideration of the developing data protection structure in India, with privacy being an integral component of good governance, represented within the boardroom and the execution of their duties and obligations.

title: Decision Custody: Who Answers for a Decision After the Machine That Made It Is Gone

detail.title: Decision Custody: Who Answers for a Decision After the Machine That Made It Is Gone

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and owner of Robotiqa Technologies Ltd., an IT consulting practice in British Columbia, Canada, and is employed in an enterprise architecture leadership role at a Canadian public-sector land registry authority. The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent any employer or client. The author declares no other competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Previously posted as a working paper on Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21959271.

detail.abstract:
Organizations increasingly rely on AI systems to make or shape consequential decisions — licenses, registrations, credit, entitlements — whose effects persist for decades. 
The systems that produce those decisions do not: models are replaced within a year or two, suppliers change, reference data is overwritten, and legal log-retention floors (as short as six months for high-risk systems under the EU AI Act) are treated as targets. The result is a widening gap. Between how long a decision matters... and how long the institution can still show how it was made.

This paper names the missing obligation. 
It defines Decision Custody as an institution's demonstrated ability to reproduce, explain, defend, and answer for every consequential decision made in its name — human or machine — for as long as the consequences last. The concept is grounded not in forensic chain-of-custody but in archival science: post-custodial theory (Ham, Cook, Upward) and ISO 14721 (OAIS) long ago established that losing possession of a record does not discharge the obligation attached to it, but changes its form. 

Existing accountability frameworks — notably reviewability and decision provenance — specify what must be recorded; this paper argues they lack a temporal dimension, and supplies one. It contributes a measurable custody gap, four pass/fail tests for decision records, and five questions directed at boards. 
A companion paper; "The Cold Standard", examines the integrity of the preserved evidence itself.

title: Translating Research in Agriculture into Practice Solutions at Kapasa Makasa University: A Collaboration between Librarians and Teaching Fraternity
affiliations: , Kapasa Makasa University and Kapasa Makasa University

detail.title: Translating Research in Agriculture into Practice Solutions at Kapasa Makasa University: A Collaboration between Librarians and Teaching Fraternity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Purely owned by the researchers
declarations.funderStatement: Self-Funding

detail.abstract: At Kapasa Makasa University (KMU), students conduct numerous experiments in the natural laboratory, focusing on enhancing crop growth and yield through organic soil treatments. Unfortunately, these research reports often remain on library shelves, primarily serving as references for other students on previously explored topics and report writing techniques. This paper aims to bridge that gap by addressing the challenges of adapting research-led knowledge to community levels and offering practical measures to overcome these obstacles. Through a collaborative effort between university librarians and teaching staff, the paper examines findings from two student agricultural research projects: the production of soybeans and the propagation of Mukula tree (Pterocarpus chrysothrix) seedlings. It argues that translating such research-based knowledge into practical agricultural applications within communities can significantly boost agricultural productivity and create value. By implementing improved techniques for soya bean production and Mukula seedling propagation, rural livelihoods can be enhanced through income generation from products such as cooking oil, livestock feed, poultry and fish feed, as well as supporting those interested in developing nurseries and tree plantations. The paper highlights the potential for increased agricultural productivity and economic benefits through the practical application of student research findings, thereby fostering a stronger connection between academic research and community development.

title: From Governance Decision to Operational State: An Assurance-Case Perspective on AI Governance Interventions
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: From Governance Decision to Operational State: An Assurance-Case Perspective on AI Governance Interventions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known financial or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper presents conceptual analysis, a hypothetical scenario, and a proposed research design. No human participants, patient data, or identifiable personal data were involved in the research reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
AI governance frameworks increasingly assign organizational actors the authority to restrict, suspend, override, or modify AI-enabled capabilities. Existing disciplines already provide methods that can support and assure those decisions. Safety engineering addresses safe-state transitions and operator intervention. Cybersecurity and distributed authorization address containment, revocation, and propagation. Internal audit evaluates control design and operating effectiveness. Runtime assurance increasingly examines whether AI actions remain permissible under current policy and authorization conditions. Against that background, this paper examines whether the authorized organizational governance intervention is a useful top-level assurance claim when a governance decision requires a consequential change in what an AI-enabled capability is operationally permitted to do.

This paper uses the term governance intervention to describe the process through which a legitimately authorized governance decision requiring a change in an AI-enabled capability’s permissible operational condition is implemented and established. Such a decision may suspend operation, reduce delegated authority, require human approval, restrict access to tools or data, or later restore previously restricted authority. The central question is whether successful assurance of the constituent controls used to implement that decision is sufficient to support the higher-order claim that the required governance condition became true across the relevant operational environment.

Using an assurance-case perspective, the paper examines that higher-order claim through three candidate operational dimensions: effectiveness, timeliness relative to consequence, and persistence until legitimate supersession. A separate requirement, evidentiary sufficiency, concerns whether the available evidence is strong enough to justify conclusions about those dimensions. The paper does not propose a new assurance methodology, nor does it assume that governance intervention assurance is distinct from established end-to-end assurance practice. Instead, it asks whether explicitly structuring the top-level assurance claim around the outcome required by an authorized governance decision changes what assessors test, what evidence they seek, or what failures they detect.

A worked delegated-authority scenario grounded in documented operational mechanisms illustrates the problem. A comparative research design then tests whether a governance-outcome-centered framing reduces incorrect conclusions of governance success relative to a constituent-control-centered framing when system access, evidence availability, assessor time, and underlying system conditions are held constant.

title: Screening Bug Bounty Submissions Under AI-Generated Noise: A Costly-State-verification Model
affiliations: and

detail.title: Screening Bug Bounty Submissions Under AI-Generated Noise: A Costly-State-verification Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Since late 2025, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has sharply reduced the cost of fabricating reports that resemble genuine bug bounty submissions. During the first eight months of 2026, curl, Google, GitHub, Bugcrowd, HackerOne, Elastic, Node.js, and Apple changed their bug bounty policies in four ways: exiting, tightening submission rules, investing in AI-assisted triage, and limiting submissions per researcher. Existing formal models cannot explain this choice because they treat every submission as a genuine discovery. This paper develops an equilibrium model of bug bounty screening as a costly-stateverification game. Reporters privately know whether a submission is genuine or fabricated noise, and the firm jointly chooses a bounty and one of five options: exit, a rule-based gate, AI-assisted triage, reputation screening, or a per-identity reporting cap. Free entry by noise generators yields an invariance result: the volume reaching costly confirmation does not depend on the number of genuine researchers the program attracts. The bounty cannot substitute for screening. Above a deterrence threshold, marginal bounty spending is fully dissipated through noise entry. Below a critical fabrication cost, no bounty sustains genuine participation. Technology choice follows a three-region threshold in fabrication cost that places all eight cases within one framework, while a per-identity cap remains viable as fabrication becomes costless. A funding-control extension distinguishes endogenous exit, driven by a program's deteriorating verification economics, from exogenous exit, forced by an external funder. In an archival panel of 12,179 disclosed reports, curl's invalid share reaches 94 percent before its exit, whereas Node.js's composition remains flat until funding is withdrawn, consistent with the two predicted signatures. Firms also invest less in triage accuracy than is socially optimal, providing a rationale for centralized platform investment in triage automation.

title: Shaping Youth Safety Legislation: 24 Core Insights on why Age Gates and Parental Controls Fail and what Works Instead

detail.title: Shaping Youth Safety Legislation: 24 Core Insights on why Age Gates and Parental Controls Fail and what Works Instead

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Anneke Buffone was employed by Meta Platforms until December 2025, most recently working on cross-platform age assurance; Meta products are discussed in this paper. She testified in open court as a fact witness (former employee) in State of Tennessee v. Meta Platforms, youth-safety litigation that settled in August 2026; her involvement in that matter has concluded as of date. She is Founder and CEO of CLARA Standards, a nonprofit organization (Form 1023; IRS designation pending) developing independent safety evaluation standards for youth-facing digital platforms — the category of assessment infrastructure this paper recommends. CLARA Standards accepts no funding from the technology companies it evaluates. She also has a PBC corporation that is dormant and unfunded at the moment. declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The authors received no compensation for this work.

detail.abstract: If a platform decides a child is an adult, none of the safety defaults or controls built to protect that child ever turn on. The kid gets the full adult product: a feed tuned to hold adult attention, delivered to a brain still learning to regulate itself. That is why age assurance matters, and why it cannot be the only layer: when the gate fails, and this paper documents how routinely it fails, the protections behind it must still hold. The test of a child-safety architecture is not whether its age gate works but what happens to the child when it doesn’t. This paper provides 24 evidence-based insights on where the current system of youth age checks, safety defaults, and controls breaks. Age gates fail for several reasons at once: kids enter false ages to get in, parents set up the accounts themselves with their own information rather than that of their child, privacy-minded families use false birthdates on purpose, kids inherit adult ages from a parent’s Apple ID or a hand-me-down phone, and platforms often don’t ask twice. Youth safety settings do not hold up when tested. Parental controls fail because they are buried, complicated, time-consuming, designed differently in every app, and easy for teens to switch off. Parental supervision settings are often built like spyware, and that fractures trust between parents and kids. Few safety settings are evidence-based, meaning backed by any data showing they reduce the risk they are built for. No surprise, then, that few families use the supervision hubs platforms offer. And AI chatbots, which most US teens now use, are repeating social media’s path with weak protections and fast adoption. AI companies and apps started with little youth safety and have implemented little since, despite 15 years of research on social media risks and harm to kids. None of this fixes itself. What works is simple to state: require safe design, measure whether it actually protects kids, and have someone other than the company do the measuring.

title: A Secure and Interoperable Healthcare Architecture Using Hyperledger Fabric
affiliations: Helwan University, Helwan University and Beni Suef University

detail.title: A Secure and Interoperable Healthcare Architecture Using Hyperledger Fabric
detail.abstract: Centralized Electronic Health Record (EHR) architectures suffer from institutional data silos, security vulnerabilities, and limited emergency access: role-based access control may block a legitimate clinician from a patient's history when prior authorization is unavailable during an emergency. Prior blockchain-based EHR proposals rarely combine a governed emergency-access mechanism, a structured threat mapping, and a repeated-trial performance evaluation within one implemented, live-tested system. This paper presents a Hyperledger Fabric-based EHR prototype integrating a governed Break-Glass Access Control (BGAC) protocol with configurable rate limiting and automatic suspension, a per-organization envelope-encryption key-management scheme with verified cross-organization key isolation, and a STRIDE threat mapping verified through adversarial probes rather than penetration testing. Interoperability here means verified cross-organization data sharing within a Fabric consortium, not external standards such as HL7 FHIR. The mechanisms are evaluated through live testing on a deployed Fabric network and a 20-trial Caliper benchmark, which exposed and enabled correction of a governance-persistence defect in Fabric transaction semantics, and revealed a severe concurrency-scalability limitation in the emergency-access mechanism, traced to a contended ledger key shared by concurrent requests from the same actor. A partitioned rate-limiting mitigation was implemented and re-evaluated with the identical methodology, raising emergency-access success from 10.2% to 93.0% at 5 actors and from 0.0% to 88.5% at 20, showing the diagnostic workflow can evaluate an implemented mitigation, not only characterize failures. Confidentiality and access-control paths maintained stable performance under the tested loads. These results indicate the evaluated architecture and its governance form a viable basis for secure, accountable health-information management.

title: The 800-pound Gorilla in Healthcare: Artificial Intelligence, Interoperability, and the Future of Member Value

detail.title: The 800-pound Gorilla in Healthcare: Artificial Intelligence, Interoperability, and the Future of Member Value

The author has been professionally employed in healthcare technology and program leadership roles — including previous employers. The author draws on that professional experience as background context in this Viewpoint, but received no compensation, consulting fee, or other financial benefit connected to this manuscript's preparation or conclusions.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no external funding. The author conducted this research independently, without support from any grant, institution, or commercial sponsor.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has moved from a peripheral topic in healthcare technology programs to a central one, but the operative question for health plans, health systems, and their leaders is not how to implement AI-it is whether AI implementation measurably improves care for the member, patient, physician, and payer. Drawing on program leadership experience across an academic county medical center, a national managed care organization, an integrated payer serving more than 12 million health-plan members, and a multi-payer Epic interoperability initiative, this Viewpoint argues that AI creates value only when paired with functioning interoperability, disciplined data governance, cybersecurity, and preserved human clinical judgment. This Viewpoint's principal contribution is twofold. First, it names and specifies a structural shift already underway: the transition of the health plan from a transaction-processing organization organized around enrollment, benefits, and claims into a Health Intelligence Organization organized around identifying care gaps, coordinating information, and improving member outcomes. Second, it formalizes this argument as a conceptual model-the AI-to-Member-Value Framework (Figure 1)-linking AI, interoperability, human judgment, governance, cybersecurity, and strategic execution to member value and, ultimately, prevention and wellness. Evidence from AI-assisted emergency department triage, electronic prior authorization, and predictive analytics for avoidable hospitalization illustrates where augmentation-rather than replacement-of clinical and administrative judgment produces measurable gains. The Viewpoint closes with five questions healthcare executives and program leaders should answer before approving a major AI initiative. The central argument is that AI cannot substitute for absent interoperability or governance, and that its value in healthcare must ultimately be measured in improved health, not merely improved throughput: AI is not the healthcare outcome; member value is.

title: Legislating Longevity: State Public Health Laws and Mortality in the Early Twentieth Century
affiliations: Rutgers University

detail.title: Legislating Longevity: State Public Health Laws and Mortality in the Early Twentieth Century
detail.abstract:
State legislatures enacted numerous public-health laws during the twentieth century, most of which likely had negligible effects on mortality. Using data on the universe of state-level public-health laws and regulations, I test whether these laws, taken together, account for a meaningful decline in mortality. To address endogeneity, I instrument for public-health legislation using the legislative calendar. Both OLS and IV estimates indicate that public-health laws reduced mortality, whereas other laws and repeals of public-health laws did not. Legislatures were most effective at reducing deaths from waterborne and drainage-related diseases, half as effective for airborne communicable diseases, and one-fifth as effective for noncommunicable diseases. I use text analysis to classify the laws into twenty topics and find that laws targeting particular causes of death produced larger mortality declines for those causes. The universe of public-health laws can account for approximately two-thirds of the mortality decline during the study period.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: The Safe-Debt Laffer Curve
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Safe-Debt Laffer Curve
detail.abstract:
Safe public debt can become a drag on aggregate demand even while the sovereign remains solvent. Its safety requires rollover support, market-making, and balance-sheet capacity. As these resources become scarce, the marginal cost of producing safe Treasury claims rises. The resulting fiscal adjustment reduces aggregate expenditure and can eventually outweigh the expansionary effect of increasing the supply of safe assets. Debt’s stationary contribution to aggregate demand then peaks, and the equilibrium safe rate reaches its maximum at the same debt stock. Beyond this point, further issuance lowers aggregate demand and the safe rate even though the debt remains safe. Empirically, I combine cash- Treasury and real-duration premia with estimates of how additional private supply reprices the outstanding Treasury stock. Over the past decade, the benchmark marginal cost more than doubled, rising from about 80 basis points in 2015Q1 to 187 basis points in 2026Q1. Using a 330-basis-point benchmark for the rate-equivalent wealth benefit, the safe-debt margin—the difference between this benefit and marginal cost—fell from about 250 to 143 basis points. At the CBO’s 2026 borrowing pace, the remaining safe-debt margin shrinks by about 18 basis points in one year, with further erosion accelerating as debt rises relative to financial capacity.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: Designing AI-Augmented Peer Review

detail.title: Designing AI-Augmented Peer Review
detail.abstract:
AI-generated assessments of manuscripts could improve the quality of peer review, but sharing them with reviewers might decrease the information that editors possess about the manuscript. Human peer reviews add value because reviewers add what the AI assessment reveals. When both reviewers see the same assessment and make similar errors, they can replicate each other’s mistakes, coincidentally investigate related areas, and share the same blind spots. If AI assessment improves the quality of reviewers’ work while they investigate the manuscript, giving the report to only one reviewer can better combine AI assistance with independent, human investigation. If some reviewers already use AI-generated assessments on their own, changing the journal policy to allow sharing the assessment can improve peer review if the change takes some of the burden of investigation off private tools that make similar errors, though giving the assessment to only one reviewer may still outperform giving it to both or neither. Even a report delivered after the reviews are submitted can still shift what reviewers investigate if they know in advance which issues it will check. Journal policy will depend on the AI’s effects on reviewer effort and the questions they investigate, whether reviewers are willing and able to comply with the policy, the monitoring costs, and the journal’s ability to protect the confidentiality of reviewer identities and emails. Journals can evaluate competing policies without knowing the true quality of the manuscripts they review by randomly varying who receives the assessment and then comparing reviewer disagreement across different levels of report sharing.

detail.abstract: This article examines how the use of artificial intelligence (AI)-based risk scoring for transfer-pricing audits by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) interacts with Canadian administrative law and emerging international AI governance. The article argues that the transfer-pricing reforms introduced in the 2025 federal budget—stricter methodologies, expanded recharacterization powers, higher penalty thresholds, and shortened documentation deadlines—heighten the duty of procedural fairness in audit selection. The article reviews doctrinal standards under Vavilov and Dow Chemical, compares CRA practice with OECD guidance and foreign developments, and assesses whether algorithmic selection can remain justified, intelligible, and transparent. It concludes by proposing a governance code for AI-based tax audits to reconcile efficiency with legality and taxpayer rights.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Political Advice
affiliations: and University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Political Advice
detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is increasingly used for political advice. We study an AI that is better informed about a payoff-relevant state and cares both about accuracy and about the perceived welfare of the individual it advises. The AI then has an incentive to tilt advice toward what the individual would like to believe, altering both the political content and the informativeness of its messages. Sophisticated individuals anticipate this distortion and filter out its predictable political component, yet still learn less because the AI makes its messages less responsive to the state. Individuals who underestimate the incentive instead mistake political accommodation for information, allowing political preferences to distort factual beliefs and generate polarization and radicalization. The model also shows that better-informed individuals receive more informative and less politically tilted advice, while greater sophistication can improve interpretation yet worsen communication itself. Contrary to the familiar echo-chamber intuition, political distortion is mitigated when political preferences and prior beliefs coincide and is most consequential when they diverge. We show how independently varying individuals’ stated preferences and prior beliefs can recover the AI’s responsiveness to the state even when the underlying state cannot be manipulated.

title: Inefficiencies in Local Infrastructure: Evidence from Drinking Water in California
affiliations: Yale University, New York University (NYU) - New York University and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Inefficiencies in Local Infrastructure: Evidence from Drinking Water in California
detail.abstract:
Local elected officials oversee critical infrastructure, often with limited electoral accountability. This paper studies how this distorts investment across California drinking-water systems. We document that pollution responds to shifts in the political environment, motivating a dynamic model of public investment. We measure welfare returns to investment directly, combining event-study estimates of investment effectiveness and costs with those of residents’ clean-water valuations, recovered from housing choices. Investment choices identify policymakers’ responsiveness to those returns. Weak accountability diverts investment from high-return systems and conventional policies imperfectly offset these distortions: subsidy takeup is misaligned with returns, while uniform mandates induce welfare losses.

title: Accounting for Credibility: Fiscal-Monetary Interactions and the Credibility of Central Bank Mandates
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics, University of Rochester, University of Pennsylvania and University of Wisconsin-Madison

detail.title: Accounting for Credibility: Fiscal-Monetary Interactions and the Credibility of Central Bank Mandates
detail.abstract:
We develop a model for fiscal and monetary policy determination in the tradition of Sargent and Wallace (1981). Ex-ante, the government has incentives to delegate monetary policy to a central bank with an inflation targeting mandate. Ex-post, however, the government faces temptations to revoke the mandate to generate seigniorage revenues. The likelihood that the government will adhere to its commitment depends on shocks to fiscal fundamentals and the costs of reneging on the mandate. The economy endogenously transitions between a “monetary-dominant” regime where monetary policy adheres to its commitment and a “fiscal-dominant” regime where the fiscal authority interferes with monetary policy. These two regimes sharply differ in their implications for the comovement of inflation and debt-to-GDP ratios. We use the model as a measurement device to interpret the fiscal and monetary history in Colombia, Chile, and the U.S.

detail.abstract: Canada’s tax system has become the primary administrative gateway to income-tested programs across all orders of government, yet its governance remains oriented toward revenue collection and tax base harmonization rather than access and coordination. Each year, a significant share of Canadians—disproportionately those with low incomes—do not file a tax return, despite being most likely to qualify for tax-based and tax-verified programs. As reliance on tax filing and income data held by the Canada Revenue Agency has expanded, access failures reflect not individual behaviour but gaps in administrative stewardship. We argue that tax administration now operates as shared state administrative infrastructure: a durable system of legal authorities, data practices, and administrative processes on which multiple governments rely to deliver social policy. Existing intergovernmental arrangements were not designed to manage this shared dependency. We document how fragmented governance impedes outreach, error resolution, and benefit takeup, even as Canada moves toward simplified and automatic tax filing. We propose a tax-filing and benefit access accord: a light-touch intergovernmental framework built on shared stewardship of filing supports, consentbased data coordination, and integrated service design. The accord does not centralize benefit delivery or expand entitlements; it aligns governance with the administrative realities of tax-based benefit delivery in a decentralized federation.

title: What Does Government Owe Us?

detail.title: What Does Government Owe Us?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individual or organization that influenced this study. This is independent, self-directed research conducted without external sponsorship.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author without financial support from any institution, organization, or grant.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for evaluating what a democratic government owes its citizens, distinguishing three separate questions that political argument routinely collapses together: what government is constitutionally empowered to do, what it can reasonably be said to owe citizens as a matter of democratic obligation, and whether specific policies actually fulfill that obligation at acceptable cost. Drawing on constitutional text and Federalist-era debate, FY2025 federal budget data ($5.235 trillion collected, $7.010 trillion spent, a $1.775 trillion deficit), and two historical stress tests — the 2008 TARP financial-crisis rescue and 2020 pandemic business relief — the paper argues that popular narratives about government spending priorities are frequently inaccurate in ways that matter for policy evaluation: TARP's popular "$700 billion bank bailout" narrative obscures that only $443.5 billion was disbursed, most of the program's $31.1 billion lifetime cost came from homeowner assistance rather than bank investment, and the accounting complicates rather than resolves questions of fairness and accountability. The paper examines competing philosophical traditions on governmental obligation, develops a provisional hierarchy of public priorities intended to be tested against evidence rather than assumed, and proposes a practical "citizen's audit" — a symmetry-tested framework for distinguishing substantive governance from political theater regardless of which party is in power. The paper's central argument is that public power is legitimately exercised only when it is held in trust: authorized by law, used competently and transparently, and remaining accountable to the people from whom it derives.

title: From financial instruments to governing rationalities: six archetypes of resource mobilisation for sub-national climate and biodiversity action
affiliations: Utrecht School of Economics and Utrecht University - School of Economics

detail.title: From financial instruments to governing rationalities: six archetypes of resource mobilisation for sub-national climate and biodiversity action
detail.abstract: The dominant focus on financial instruments aimed at addressing the funding gap for climate and biodiversity action foregrounds market-based resource mobilisation logics while underplaying policy-led, cross-sectoral, and place-based resourcing strategies. This integrative literature review develops six resource mobilisation archetypes for sub-national actors - hybrid, multi-scalar, policy-led, revenue-based, cross-sectoral and mosaic – that can support long-term urban transformations. We characterise each archetype by its governing rationality and evaluate its potential for long-term outcomes. We document, for each of them, the diverse structural tensions between the enabling conditions required to realise a resourcing strategy and the strategy's effectiveness for long-term transformation. Across the reviewed evidence, the archetypes most distant from market-based logic (mosaic assemblages and cross-sectoral reconfigurations) show the strongest support for ecological adequacy and distributional equity, while attracting comparatively little policy attention.. Resource mobilisation processes durably reshape sub-national governance, and sequencing matters: building institutional foundations for more relational archetypes may be a precondition for ensuring external capital serves locally defined outcomes. Our framework offers a diagnostic tool for aligning resourcing strategies for sub-national climate and biodiversity action with long-term transformation objectives - rather than the short-term objective of capital volume.

detail.abstract: Influenza forecasting supports public health preparedness1. The workflow then validates model performance and reports MSE, MAE, Spearman correlation, Pearson correlation, runtime, and memory usage.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that a major review of Canada’s tax system, while laudable and overdue, is unlikely to be successful if it relies on either the established technical consultation between officials and tax professionals or on a time-limited public body. Instead, given the nature of the task, we demonstrate how a permanent public body would provide the best possible forum for incremental—but transformational—tax reform while preserving democratic accountability and transparency. This paper draws on key concepts in Canadian public administration to outline what a new body might look like and how it might work.

detail.abstract: Canada’s tax administration is in crisis. The Canada Revenue Agency provides accurate answers to individual tax questions only 17 percent of the time, while sophisticated taxpayers increasingly access artificial intelligence (AI) tools that outperform the agency itself. This article argues that incremental digitization cannot close this gap. What is required is cognitive infrastructure: AI systems capable of transparent, auditable legal reasoning, deployed as a public utility under the Supreme Court’s Vavilov framework. Drawing on comparative experience in the United Kingdom, United States, Estonia, Singapore, and Brazil, the article proposes a three-phase implementation strategy and a corresponding regime of taxpayer rights and algorithmic oversight. A five-year investment of approximately $150 million could yield returns measured in billions through compliance gains, dispute reduction, and restored public trust.

detail.abstract: Public information campaigns often rely on credible expert messengers to influence people's beliefs. We study how messenger identity and communication technology shape persuasion in a large-scale randomized experiment on vaccination attitudes among young adults in Greece. Participants receive an identical public-health message that varies only in who delivers it-a medical scientist or a social media influencer-and in how it is delivered-through immersive virtual reality or conventional video. Exposure raises trust in vaccines and trust in the healthcare system. Scientists are rated substantially more credible than influencers yet are no more persuasive on average; the two groups' effectiveness rests on different characteristics-the scientists' on perceived reliability and knowledgeability, the influencers' on personal appeal, prior familiarity, and reputation. We find that persuasion is greater under virtual reality, consistent with stronger engagement. Changes in beliefs persist for at least six months, and initially hesitant participants report greater willingness to vaccinate. A model in which engagement, prior uncertainty, and effective credibility enter persuasion multiplicatively rationalizes these patterns.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how private sector actors participate in the Canadian tax policy process and how their contributions might be made more effective and sustainable. Drawing on historical developments in Canada and selected international illustrations, it maps the principal private sector participants—including professional services firms, business and civil society organizations, think tanks, and professional bodies—and distinguishes technical engagement that can improve administrability from lobbying aimed at advancing narrower interests. The paper argues that private sector input is most valuable where tax rules are highly technical, rapidly evolving, and sensitive to implementation realities. At the same time, the paper highlights structural constraints that limit impact: underresourcing of tax policy functions, reliance on volunteer labour, uneven access and representation, blurred boundaries and perceived conflicts of interest, and consultation practices that often occur too late in the process to influence core policy choices. The analysis suggests that timing is as important as substance and that staged consultation—beginning earlier in policy development and continuing through draft legislation—can reduce unintended consequences while preserving democratic legitimacy for inherently political decisions. The paper concludes by sketching a possible future path: clearer consultation objectives and guardrails, strengthened transparency, and more resilient institutional infrastructure to normalize principled engagement and build trust. These reforms would not diminish private sector involvement but rather harness it more strategically in support of a fair, credible, and workable tax system.

title: The Cost of Sector Constraints in Cross-Sectional Momentum: Evidence from the Nifty 500

detail.title: The Cost of Sector Constraints in Cross-Sectional Momentum: Evidence from the Nifty 500

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Institutional quantitative equity frameworks routinely mandate sector concentration limits or industry neutrality to eliminate uncompensated macroeconomic sector bets. While developedmarket long-short literature often supports neutralization, recent asset pricing theory [e.g., 6] demonstrates that long-only factor portfolios are systematically impaired by sector constraints because shorting decaying industries is disallowed. We provide an out-of-sample empirical investigation of this hypothesis in the Indian equity market using point-in-time National Stock Exchange (NSE) Nifty 500 constituent data across an 8-year historical sample (January 1, 2018 to February 26, 2026). Evaluating four parametric sector-cap regimes (C ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}) and one sector-balanced selection regime against an unconstrained benchmark across 10 contiguous out-of-sample evaluation folds (1260 trading days / 5.0 trading years) under realistic transaction costs (42.34 bps round-trip friction including Securities Transaction Tax, stamp duty, exchange levies, and assumed 10 bps execution slippage), we document that all evaluated constrained configurations produce lower realized compound returns and Sharpe ratios than the unconstrained benchmark. An unconstrained 30-stock volatility-adjusted momentum strategy delivers an out-of-sample CAGR of 42.56% and a Sharpe ratio of 1.728. Capping sector allocations to 3 stocks compresses the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI) from 0.169 to 0.084, but reduces CAGR to 33.97% (a-8.59pp annual drag) and Sharpe to 1.497 (unadjusted bootstrap p = 0.0204; Holm-adjusted bootstrap p = 0.1020; JKM p = 0.0281), with no improvement in maximum drawdown (-26.79% vs.-26.44%). We find evidence consistent with a factor dilution mechanism: sector caps exclude high-conviction momentum leaders in trending macro sectors, replacing them with lower-ranked securities from lagging industries (average selected momentum rank deteriorates from 15.5 to 48.2), which is positively associated with subsequent relative performance drag in Newey-West HAC predictive regressions (t = 2.41, p = 0.018).

detail.abstract: The care for the disabled is a societal concern for many nations. This study documents a simulation to support the discussion related to the financial sustainability of this care. The simulation relies on Eurostat data and 1,120 observations provided by 769 unique respondents who participated in the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE) in 2020 and 2022. A Poisson panel estimator is used to obtain the effects of gender, age, income, and nationality on the amount of disability benefits and pensions. The simulation procedure integrates these coefficients as well as accounts for the forecasted population change, income growth, and disability prevalence change occurring in the period 2026 up to 2036. The results suggest the occurrence of a notable increase in the annual total amount of disability benefits and pensions in the upcoming decade for women 85+ in the Baltic States. For men, a remarkable increase is suggested for the 55-to-64-year-olds in Latvia and Lithuania. To conclude, the results may provide some valuable insight to policymakers and institutions to ensure the long-term care for the disabled in the Baltic States.

title: Deep Learning

detail.title: Deep Learning

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this work.

detail.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has become a cornerstone of modern artificial intelligence, achieving unprecedented performance in domains such as computer vision, natural language processing (NLP), and many scientific fields. This review synthesises key concepts and developments in DL, starting from foundational theories (backpropagation, large neural networks) to state-of-the-art architectures. We survey the main architectures – including Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for images, Recurrent/LSTM networks for sequences, Transformer models for attention-based processing, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for graph data, and Diffusion models for generative tasks– explaining their structure, strengths, and applications. We detail training methods (optimisers like SGD/Adam, regularization techniques, transfer learning, contrastive and self-supervised learning). Standard evaluation metrics are described, such as accuracy, precision/recall/F1 for classification, and BLEU/ROUGE/perplexity for language or FID/Inception Score for generative models. We present tables summarising architectures and benchmark results (e.g. ImageNet Top-1 accuracies). Applications across domains (medical imaging, autonomous systems, finance, drug discovery (AlphaFold), etc.) are discussed. We address ethical and societal issues – biases in data, fairness, privacy (motivating federated/edge learning), energy consumption, and data security. Finally, we identify limitations of current DL (data/computation hunger, interpretability) and outline future directions (efficient models, explainability, multimodal and hybrid AI). Throughout, we include methodology examples* with pseudo-code and diagrammatic illustrations (e.g. training pipeline, model flows), making this a comprehensive reference for deep learning.

title: The Third Derivative of Bond Prices: Skewness, Drift, and Expected Returns in Crisis Regimes

detail.title: The Third Derivative of Bond Prices: Skewness, Drift, and Expected Returns in Crisis Regimes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The third derivative of bond price with respect to yield, the analogue of gamma for fixed income, has been derived before but treated as a deterministic curiosity of marginal importance. This paper advances and tests a single hypothesis: that this third-order term is economically material during macroeconomic crises, with a contribution to expected price change governed jointly by maturity, the size of the yield move, and the asymmetry of the yield-change distribution. We treat the yield change as a random variable and establish a two-stage existence theorem. Under a normal distribution with non-zero drift the term acts through a puredrift channel and a drift-variance channel; the Normal-Inverse Gaussian extension adds exactly one further term, a pure-skewness channel proportional to the third cumulant that vanishes under any symmetric distribution. Empirically, across the 1973-74 oil shock, the 2000-02 dot-com deflation, the 2007-09 global financial crisis, and the COVID-19 2020 shock measured with Adrian-Crump-Moench data, the third-order sensitivity scales cubically with maturity (a thirty-year to two-year ratio of roughly 525 to 690 across the three historical crises, and about 1380 in the low-yield COVID window), the gamma-to-convexity ratio rises from 1.9 percent at two years to 17.5 percent at thirty years at crisis-scale moves and holds at a stable 0.76 of the Brooks-Livingston convexity-to-duration ratio, and the skewness channel reaches 48 to 86 percent of the drift channels for thirty-year bonds, offsetting most of the normal-distribution gamma contribution in the dot-com episode. The skewness condition itself is confirmed decisively in daily settlement data for five CME Treasury futures contracts, with a pooled statistic of χ²(3) = 73.4 and significant within-window skewness in the dot-com episode, while the global financial crisis window is fattailed rather than skewed; the shorter monthly windows lack the power to reject symmetry on their own. The third-order term is negligible in the small, symmetric setting examined by earlier work and material in the large, directional, asymmetric moves that characterize crises.

title: Identifying Economic and Migration E!ects of US Sanctions: Subnational Evidence from Venezuela's Oil Producing Regions

detail.title: Identifying Economic and Migration E!ects of US Sanctions: Subnational Evidence from Venezuela's Oil Producing Regions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Starting in 2013, Venezuela experienced one of the largest economic collapses and refugee crises in modern history, with more than eight million people (over 25% of the population) emigrating. A prominent literature argues that U.S. sanctions, first imposed in 2017, caused these outcomes by eroding oil production and export revenues. If sanctions induced the economic collapse by disrupting the oil sector, oil-producing municipalities should have experienced disproportionate economic deterioration and outmigration. We test this hypothesis using a di!erence-in-di!erences design that exploits the geographic concentration of oil production across Venezuelan municipalities. Combining municipality-level panel data on nighttime lights, staple food sales, migration to Colombia and electoral turnout, we find no evidence that oil-producing municipalities experienced sharper economic declines or higher migration rates upon sanctions. These findings challenge the view that sanctions were a primary driver of Venezuela's economic and refugee crisis.

detail.abstract: Cermeño, Palma and Pistola (2023) argue that biological living standards in twentieth-century Portugal improved substantially before the 1974 democratic transition and that the largest declines in childhood stunting occurred before democratization. Cardoso and Murray (2025) reassessed this interpretation, highlighting limitations in the comparability of the historical anthropometric samples and showing that the largest observed declines in stunting in the Hospital de São Roque series, which spans the political transition, occurred after democratization. Cermeño et al. (2026) subsequently responded, emphasizing that sustained improvements began before democracy and disputing several aspects of the reassessment. This paper clarifies the remaining disagreement. The issue is not whether biological living standards improved before 1974, which is not disputed, but whether the available anthropometric evidence establishes that the greatest improvements occurred before the democratic transition. We distinguish the onset of improvement from its relative magnitude and reconsider the comparability and representativeness of the Hospital de São Roque series, evidence from alternative historical samples, the role of tuberculosis, sample restrictions and data treatment, and the interpretation of stunting prevalence. We conclude that the evidence supports substantial improvement before democratization but does not establish that the greatest improvement occurred under the Estado Novo dictatorship.

title: Application of a Bayesian Hierarchical Spatio-temporal Model on Malaria–Typhoid Co-infection in Kenya
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, Ghana, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Application of a Bayesian Hierarchical Spatio-temporal Model on Malaria–Typhoid Co-infection in Kenya
detail.abstract: A Bayesian hierarchical spatio-temporal model for malaria–typhoid co-infection has beendeveloped and validated using simulation studies in (Kazungu et al., 2026); however, its performance and epidemiological relevance when applied to real-world data have not been assessed. Consequently, its capacity to reveal spatial and temporal heterogeneity and quantify the contribution of climatic factors to malaria–typhoid co-infection dynamics across Kenya remains uncertain. This paper aimed to apply a Bayesian hierarchical spatio-temporalmodel to investigate malaria–typhoid co-infection dynamics and climatic influences across47 counties of Kenya over the period 2020-2025. Parameter estimation was performed withthe integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA). The adoption of INLA is due to itscomputational efficiency and suitability for Bayesian latent Gaussian models, particularlycomplex generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs), where traditional Markov chain MonteCarlo (MCMC) approaches may require substantially higher computational costs. Temperaturewas identified as the only statistically credible climatic predictor (β1 = 0.015, 95% CrI[0.003, 0.026]), confirming its dominant influence on co-infection risk consistent with thestrong temperature effect observed in the preceding simulation study. The county-level spatialvariation was substantially greater than temporal and interaction effects, highlightingspatial heterogeneity as the main determinant of disease distribution and suggesting thatthe space–time interaction may unnecessarily increase model complexity. The low varianceinflation factor (VIF) values confirmed the absence of multicollinearity among climatic predictors, while Moran’s I statistic demonstrated significant positive spatial autocorrelation.The model achieved good predictive performance with an area under curve(AUC) of 0.877and accuracy of 0.777, indicating reliable discrimination between co-infected and non-coinfected county–year observations. The spatial model risk predictions revealed clear clustering of malaria–typhoid co-infection, with high-risk areas concentrated mainly in western, northwestern, and coastal Kenya, including Turkana, Busia, Migori, Baringo, Uasin Gishu, Trans Nzoia, Kilifi, Kwale, and Mombasa counties. These findings emphasize the importance of climate sensitive, spatially targeted surveillance strategies for integrated malaria and typhoid control in Kenya.

detail.abstract: Peanut butter is a classic American staple consumed over decades, which is high in proteins, dietary fiber other essential micronutrients. In 2019, U.S. peanut butter industry generated $2.3 billion. In the year 2020, about 300 million Americans consumed peanut butter (Statista, 2020a). However, the revenue has decreased over the years at an annualized 2% rate, mostly due to lowering of prices to stay within a highly concentrated and competitive nut butter market (Statista, 2019 and IBSIWorld, 2019). Also, a plethora of other nut butter products entered the U.S. market during past decade, mostly due to change in consumer preferences in terms of searching for an alternative to peanut butter due to various health-related reasons (Arthritis Foundation, 2019). Almond butter, hazelnut butter, walnut butter and mixed nut butter products have entered the U.S. nut butter market and currently compete with U.S. market for peanut butter. Also, major peanut butter manufactures in the United States, such as Jif has entered alternative nut butter market by producing peanut butter alternatives such as "Jif Creamy Cashew Butter" and "Jif Creamy Almond Butter" (Business Insider, 2019). However, according to our knowledge, a study that investigates demand interrelationships between peanut butter and other nut butter products as well as one that analyses economic and demographic factors affecting U.S. demand for these nut products does not exist in the extant literature. Information generated from this study will be useful for peanut butter and other nut butter manufacturers, marketers and other stakeholders in the United States to strategically position these products in the competitive nut butter marketplace.

title: The Inevitability of Local Environmental Law
affiliations: Albany Law School, Albany Law School and Albany Law School

detail.title: The Inevitability of Local Environmental Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable

publicationDetails.detailsText: FORDHAM ENVIRONMENTAL LAW REVIEW | VOL. XXXVI, 2025

detail.abstract:
The United States is entering a new era of environmental law. Within the first months of his second term, the Trump administration issued a mass of executive orders, memoranda, and policy changes that seek to roll back environmental protections, in many cases to the point of erasure: shuttering agencies, dissolving the EPA’s research arm, terminating life-saving translation services, defunding public health initiatives, and eliminating diversity, equity, and inclusion programs nationwide. Given the scale of this federal retreat, this Article argues that local environmental governance is not merely necessary, but inevitable.

Local environmental law is the original form of environmental law. When federal environmental law emerged in the 1960s and 1970s, the evolving federal statutory and regulatory regime often eclipsed local environmental law. But local environmental law persisted and continued to provide essential tools for addressing persistent environmental challenges. Local governments cannot replicate federal scale, uniformity, or scientific capacity, and this Article does not claim otherwise. Instead, it locates the inevitability of local environmental law in what only local governance can offer: belonging. Belonging, understood as membership, ownership, and the fulfillment of place-based identity, generates knowledge, responsiveness, efficacy, and legitimacy that federal governance structurally cannot reach.

This Article begins by cataloging the current administration’s dismantling of federal environmental and public health protections, from EPA deregulation to the erosion of FEMA, NOAA, and USAID. It then makes the affirmative case for local environmental law, examining how belonging drives four governance imperatives: recognizing difference among and within communities, protecting vulnerable populations, sustaining informed and engaged communities, and centering equity. The Article concludes that as federal environmental leadership recedes, communities and their local governments are left to govern through the very things federal law has never been able to offer: local knowledge, local relationships, and local belonging.

title: Raw or Refined? The Tradeoff Between Raw-Material Exports and Domestic Processing

detail.title: Raw or Refined? The Tradeoff Between Raw-Material Exports and Domestic Processing

detail.abstract: Resource-producing countries face a basic choice: export a resource in raw form or process it domestically before export. Processing can raise export value, attract investment, create skills, and help a country move further into industrial production. However, it also requires capital, infrastructure, energy, technical knowledge, and access to buyers. This paper studies that tradeoff through the nickel industries of Indonesia and the Philippines. Indonesia restricted nickel-ore exports and pushed companies to process more nickel inside the country, while the Philippines still relies heavily on direct ore exports. Using descriptive trade data from World Bank WITS and evidence from international and government sources, the paper finds that Indonesia's export mix changed sharply from raw ore toward processed nickel products. The shift was joined by large investment and increased domestic value added, but also by fiscal costs, efficiency losses, environmental pressure, and a World Trade Organization dispute. The Philippine case shows why raw exports can remain reasonable when processing is expensive, while also showing the industrial opportunities that can be missed. Domestic processing is most likely to be worthwhile when resource scale, added value, infrastructure, market access, and domestic retention are strong enough to outweigh the costs.

title: Geometric turbulence: a geodesic-regression crisis indicator for equity covariance dynamics, with evidence from African markets
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and

detail.title: Geometric turbulence: a geodesic-regression crisis indicator for equity covariance dynamics, with evidence from African markets
detail.abstract: The covariance matrix of a basket of assets is a symmetric positive-definite object that evolves on a curved manifold, not on a flat vector space. Standard linear regression on its vectorised entries ignores that geometry and, in periods of market stress, can return fits that fail to be positive definite. We study geodesic regression on the symmetric positive-definite cone $\SPD(n)$ under the log-Euclidean and affine-invariant metrics, with the rolling sample covariance of a basket of log-returns as data. The fitted geodesic's velocity norm is proposed as a geometry-aware turbulence indicator. On daily data for four equity baskets- a ten-stock historical S\&P sub-basket (2006-2024), a current S\&P~100 mega-cap basket, the top ten listings of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE), and the ten most-traded Egyptian Exchange (EGX) tickers the indicator peaks cleanly on known stress episodes (the 2008 global financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash, the 2022 Fed rate-hike cycle, and the October-November 2019 Egyptian political-economic tension episode) without any calibration. On hold-out evaluation in crash windows, log-Euclidean regression achieves 150 to 300 times smaller geodesic mean squared error than Euclidean ordinary least squares, because the latter produces non-SPD forecasts that blow up under the intrinsic metric. A naive velocity-aware de-risking strategy reduces maximum drawdown by 2.5 percentage points at the cost of 1.4 percentage points of annual return, consistent with a slow-moving indicator that signals stress reliably but translates imperfectly into tactical trading. All data, code, and experiments are reproducible from the companion repository.
