detail.abstract: This book-length manuscript examines the political development of Barbados from Emancipation through the consolidation of modern party politics and constitutional independence. Drawing on research undertaken during the 1970s, it interprets Barbadian political change through a Marxist political-economy framework centred on class relations, productive forces, property, state power and struggles over structural transformation. Rather than presenting a chronological political history, the manuscript isolates decisive periods of conflict, including post-Emancipation resistance, the Confederation disturbances of 1876, the 1937 labour rebellion, the emergence of the labour movement, the retreat of planter government and the rise of social democratic politics. It argues that Barbados’s politics of development were shaped by persistent conflict among the plantocracy, the black and coloured underclasses, the emerging middle class and British imperial power. Particular attention is given to the distinction between political reform and substantive transformation, and to the ways constitutional advance could coexist with continuing economic concentration and class domination. The manuscript therefore challenges conventional accounts that equate institutional modernisation and Westminster-style democracy with development. By connecting political institutions to the underlying political economy, it offers a historically grounded interpretation of democratisation, decolonisation, class accommodation and the limits of post-slavery transformation in Barbados and the wider Caribbean experience.

title: Existential Non-Absorption: Freedom after Relief in the Gentle Totality
affiliations: Johann Heinrich Pestalozzi Christian University Inc.

detail.title: Existential Non-Absorption: Freedom after Relief in the Gentle Totality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract:
The article develops the concept of Existential Non-Absorption as a counter-form to Existential Alignment, as described in the preceding article. While Existential Alignment describes how human self-interpretation can be connected to AI-supported metastruc-tures and prepared plausibilities, Existential Non-Absorption asks about the possibility of living within these structures without completely merging into their relieving form of world.
At the centre stands the Gentle Totality as that operative form of the metastructure which does not primarily coerce human beings, but relieves them. Within this form, absorption does not mean mere use of technical systems or simple dependence. It means the point at which the prepared form of world loses its foreignness and becomes the self-evident space of one’s own thinking, feeling and deciding.
This article shows that this absorption does not occur only cognitively. It reaches into the reward-responsive world, in which plausibility connects to the reward model of the human being. Likewise it reaches AI-generated forms of closeness, in which comfort and stabilisation touch the self-relation. Since these aids can be real, Existential Non-Absorption cannot be understood as renunciation of technology or digital asceticism.
Existential Non-Absorption designates a figure of freedom in the midst of the Gentle Totality. The human being remains in the metastructure and uses its systems without allowing their plausibility to become the ultimate form of his self-interpretation. The article understands this attitude not as a blueprint for life and not as a programme of correct AI use, but as a freedom-theoretical boundary figure. It marks the open differ-ence between helpful stabilisation and complete absorption

title: FROM ANTICIPATION TO EMANCIPATION: HOW COMMUNITY SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY RESHAPES TERRITORIAL PROSPECTIVE IN THE COLOMBIAN ANDES
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: FROM ANTICIPATION TO EMANCIPATION: HOW COMMUNITY SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY RESHAPES TERRITORIAL PROSPECTIVE IN THE COLOMBIAN ANDES
detail.abstract: The field of futures studies has increasingly recognised the importance of anticipation as an object of inquiry, yet a critical gap persists: prevailing predictive and voluntarist frameworks fail to explain why numerous territorial prospective exercises produce scenarios that do not translate into sustained public action. This article argues that this gap is ontological, not merely methodological. Drawing on a fiveyear participatory action research study (2019–2024) in the municipality of Sutatausa, Colombia, with 372 participation records across 48 focus groups and 8 workshops (estimated unique participants: 210–250), we demonstrate that community social psychology intervention in the processes of habituation (habituación), naturalisation (naturalización) and conscientisation (concientización) (Montero, 2004) constitutes a necessary and prior condition for the effective appropriation of prospective scenarios. The article presents a fourphase model that integrates the voluntarist school (Godet, 2000, 2011) and the human and social prospective school (Barbieri Masini, 1993, 2013; Medina, 2000, 2014) with community psychosocial processes. The results show that without transforming naturalised relations of distrust, economic dependence on mining and temporal fatalism, technically robust scenarios remain powerless. We propose the concept of a relational ontology of anticipation (ontología relacional de la anticipación) as a theoretical contribution to the field, arguing that a community’s anticipatory capacity is not a predetermined cognitive attribute but an emergent property of its psychosocial configuration. The implications for territorial prospective practice are substantive: methodological design must systematically include psychosocial intervention as a prefigurative phase.

detail.abstract:
Background: Obesity affects approximately 25% of Japanese adults, although its health, economic, and fiscal burden has not been comprehensively quantified. We estimated the burden of obesity and obesity-related health disorders in Japan.

Methods: This cross-sectional modelling study, conducted on behalf of the Japan Society for the Study of Obesity, integrated DeSC claims and health check-up data from 1,127,163 individuals with national statistics and published evidence. Direct medical costs were estimated using two-part regression models. Obesity-related disorders were classified into cardiometabolic, atherosclerotic or vascular, and mechanical or structural clusters, and condition-specific costs were estimated using g-computation. Absenteeism, presenteeism, premature mortality, and government fiscal burden were estimated from claims, national statistics, and published evidence.

Finding s: Obesity-associated costs in 2025 were ¥2·75 trillion (0·4% of GDP), comprising ¥1·20 trillion in direct medical costs and ¥1·55 trillion in indirect costs. Presenteeism accounted for ¥1·23 trillion, followed by absenteeism (¥209 billion) and premature mortality (¥110 billion). The cardiometabolic cluster accounted for 81% of direct costs, alone or combined. Among disorders, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, type 2 diabetes, and musculoskeletal conditions had the largest population-level costs. We estimated 21,890 obesity-attributable deaths. Type 2 diabetes contributed most to foregone earnings from premature mortality. Government fiscal burden was ¥840 billion.

Interpretation : Obesity imposes a substantial burden across health care, productivity, and public finances. These estimates provide timely evidence for Japan's 2026 Basic Policy (Honebuto policy) on “Proactive Preventive Healthcare”, which names "obesity disease" and calls for prevention, early detection, early intervention, and behaviour change.

detail.abstract: In an age when individuals can independently learn about new products, technologies, and behaviors online, why do the adoption decisions of their real-world friends and neighbors continue to shape their own? We develop a model of social contagion in which individuals are influenced by their network neighbors but can also search for information outside the network (e.g., through online reviews). Individuals hold beliefs about the utility of adopting an innovation and update them using new information, deciding at each time step whether to adopt and whether to keep searching. The model identifies a mechanism that keeps social influence essential: individuals who are initially pessimistic about an innovation may conclude that further investigation is not worth its cost, locking themselves into non-adoption. Word-of-mouth from adopting neighbors can break this inertia and encourage further information search. The model further predicts that as the costs of acquiring and processing information fall, adoption shifts from requiring social reinforcement from multiple neighbors, as in complex contagion, to being independently triggered by a single one, as in simple contagion. Cheaper information outside the network therefore need not weaken real-world social influence; it may instead amplify the marginal impact of each adopter. These results speak to social contagion in an era when generative AI is rapidly reducing information costs.

title: Should Investment Conduct Supervision be Centralised at the EU Level? A Transaction Cost Approach Analysis

detail.title: Should Investment Conduct Supervision be Centralised at the EU Level? A Transaction Cost Approach Analysis

detail.abstract:
This research examines whether investment conduct supervision in the EU capital
market sector should be centralised at the EU level, in light of the Market Integration and
Supervision Package published in December 2025 by the European Commission. It
approaches the question through the twin-peaks supervisory framework and focuses on
investment conduct supervision as distinct from prudential supervision.
The paper applies a transaction cost approach, using the key notions of Transaction Cost
Economics as organising principles. It conducts a comparative institutional analysis
between the current supervisory system and the option of further centralising investment
conduct supervision. The central criterion is whether centralisation would produce lower
total transaction costs than the current structure.
The research identifies four sources of transaction costs within the organisational
failures framework: uncertainty/complexity, small numbers, opportunism, and bounded
rationality. It argues that investment conduct supervision has only limited cross-border
nature at the present stage. The benefits of full centralisation, such as dealing with
negative externalities and economies of scale, have therefore not yet outweighed the
heterogeneity of preferences in this area.
The analysis further suggests that Member States have different supervisory preferences,
that centralisation may increase costs arising from supervisory competition and aligned
lobbying interests, and that a decentralised structure may better preserve learning,
experimentation, diversity, and risk-sharing where supervisors are boundedly rational.
The paper concludes that centralised supervision of investment conduct at the EU level
would not reduce, and may even increase, total transaction costs. It therefore gives a
negative answer to the research question. However, this conclusion is limited: it does not
prove that the current system is optimal, nor does it exclude the possibility that other
better proposals may exist.

keywords: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999

detail.abstract: Among the grounds urged against President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's election in 2023 were three allegations bearing on section 137 of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999: that a thirty-year-old United States civil forfeiture order disqualified him under section 137(1)(d); that he held citizenship of the Republic of Guinea in addition to Nigeria; and that a certificate he presented to the electoral commission was forged. This article traces how each allegation was actually argued and determined by the Presidential Election Petition Court, drawing a sharp procedural distinction the public discourse around the case largely missed: the forfeiture allegation, raised in the Allied Peoples Movement's petition, was fully pleaded, evidenced and decided on its merits, with the tribunal engaging closely with section 137(1)(d)'s statutory language, comparative United States civil-forfeiture doctrine, and the ten-year threshold in section 137(1)(e). The citizenship and forgery allegations, by contrast, raised only in the companion Atiku Abubakar/Peoples Democratic Party petition, never reached the merits at all, struck out for having been improperly introduced through a Reply rather than the petition itself. The article closes by weighing, evenhandedly, the competing assessments of whether this outcome reflects principled constitutional textualism or an unduly narrow reading of section 137 that left serious allegations against a presidential candidate untested.

detail.abstract: Italy's fuel-tanker road haulage sector faces a structural shortage of qualified drivers, compounded by a regulatory entry barrier (Category CE driving licence, CQC professional competence certificate, ADR dangerous-goods certification) that stretches replacement timelines beyond what the ordinary labour market can absorb. This working paper evaluates six strategic alternatives: raising wages, acquisitions, importing labour, automation, external partnerships, extending the working age and argues that none resolves the structural cause (a depleting stock of qualifiable people) while retaining control over quality and cost. It proposes an alternative model, the Hybrid Driver Academy: an internal training system with merit-based selection, an economic incentive conditioned on objective criteria, and a proportional retention clause, calibrated against Italian case law on the matter and benchmarked against comparable Italian and U.S. precedents. A three-scenario analysis verifies the model's economic sustainability, and a discussion of its weaknesses, candidates left unplaced, the allocation of financial risk, completes the assessment. The paper is presented as a working proposal, with assumptions explicitly meant to be calibrated through a pilot cycle.

detail.abstract: Emerging economies pursuing national artificial intelligence agendas require a structured conceptual apparatus to reason about long-horizon trajectories of AI-driven digital transformation, yet the foresight literature offers few integrated frameworks tailored to their institutional context. This paper is a conceptual framework paper. Drawing on the Voros generic foresight process, systemic foresight, scenario analysis, morphological reasoning and the AI-assisted social media marketing framework of Basri, the paper proposes a conceptual apparatus for reasoning about AI adoption trajectories in the Republic of Kazakhstan by 2030 and derives implications for technology-society scholarship. The framework specifies two conceptual axes of uncertainty — pace of national digital infrastructure development and depth of cross-sectoral AI adoption — and articulates three illustrative scenario archetypes: accelerated national adoption, moderate sectoral progress, and delayed transformation. The applicability of the framework is discussed through four sectoral vignettes covering retail, healthcare, education and social services, with the correctional-services sector for children — illustrated by the case of ANO 'AbA — Vmeste' — analysed in greater depth to show how the framework applies to ethically sensitive, linguistically complex and institutionally constrained segments of the innovation system. A conceptual roadmap for national STI policy alignment across formative, scaling and consolidation phases is outlined as a proposal for empirical validation. The paper explicitly does not conduct a Delphi survey, a PRISMA-based systematic review, or quantitative horizon scanning; these are set out as a research agenda. The contribution is a synthesising conceptual framework that consolidates foresight scholarship for the emerging-economy AI-adoption context and provides a testable scaffold for subsequent empirical work in Kazakhstan and the wider Central Asian region.

detail.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used at work, but whether it changes workers' opportunities outside their current jobs remains unclear. We use the 2025 Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking to study workplace AI use alongside randomized hypothetical wage changes and recent labor-market outcomes. Workers respond strongly to larger wage cuts, but this response does not differ between AI users and non-users. The main difference we find relates to job search behavior: AI users are about 5 percentage points more likely to have applied for another job during the previous year. Furthermore, application rates increase with the frequency of AI use. These results suggest that workers who use generative AI at work search more actively for other jobs, although we do not find evidence that they are more likely to actually change jobs.

title: Intervention Fatigue and the Dynamics of Innovation Diffusion in Organizational Networks

detail.title: Intervention Fatigue and the Dynamics of Innovation Diffusion in Organizational Networks

declarations.declarationOfInterest: the authors declare no conflict of interest.

detail.abstract: Organizations frequently rely on repeated interventions to promote the adoption of innovative practices and behaviors. However, repeated exposure can generate intervention fatigue, making employees progressively less responsive to subsequent interventions. Existing research on innovation diffusion typically treats receptivity as a fixed individual characteristic, whereas in practice it evolves with accumulated exposure. In this paper, we specify an agent-based network model in which innovation adoption occurs through two channels: direct managerial intervention and peer influence. While the effectiveness of direct intervention declines with repeated exposure, peer influence operates through routine interactions and does not erode receptivity in the same way. We evaluate this model using three targeting strategies across synthetic and real-world interaction networks, including four intra-organizational networks, under three settings: a fatigue-free benchmark, a fatigue-blind setting in which managers ignore fatigue, and a fatigue-aware setting in which exposure history informs targeting decisions. Our results show that ignoring intervention fatigue can cause managers to substantially overestimate innovation adoption, while accounting for fatigue in targeting decisions can improve adoption by broadening intervention coverage and reducing the concentration and redundancy of intervention effort. We further show that both the cost of fatigue and the benefits of fatigue-aware targeting depend on network structure. They are greatest in hub-dominated networks, where repeated targeting rapidly exhausts influential employees, and smaller in dense networks, where peer influence plays a stronger role in adoption. This study highlights the under-discussed role of intervention fatigue in innovation network studies and offers a flexible framework for evaluating intervention outcomes when receptivity evolves with exposure.

detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is reshaping the global energy system, transforming labour markets, and rebalancing economies at a speed few anticipated. This paper synthesises current data from the International Energy Agency, the World Economic Forum, Goldman Sachs, McKinsey, the IMF, the OECD, and Anthropic's Economic Index to assess five linked questions: (I) the current and projected energy consumption of AI and data centres; (II) efficiency and productivity gains by industry sector; (III) employment displacement from repetitive and cognitive task automation; (IV) an integrated net balance sheet of costs and benefits; and (V) country-by-country estimated effects across EU Member States, the UK, the US and China. We find that global data centre electricity demand is on course to roughly double to approximately 945 TWh by 2030, driven overwhelmingly by AI workloads, while AI is simultaneously delivering measurable productivity gains-a median 30% improvement in targeted tasks-and the WEF projects 78 million net new jobs globally by 2030 alongside 92 million displaced. We argue that the net effect is likely positive at the global level, but that the distribution of costs and benefits across countries and skill groups is highly uneven, and that the policy challenge lies in managing the transition between fossil-fuel dependence and clean energy, between automation and augmentation, and between economic gains and their equitable distribution.

detail.abstract:
Purpose-This study aims to determine the role of green campus practices (GCP) on student brand advocacy (SBA), the mediating effect of institutional trust (INST.T), and the moderating role of Gen-Z environmental consciousness (GN-Z EC) within higher education institutions operating in Pakistan.

Design/methodology/approach-This study collected quantitative and cross-sectional data using structured questionnaires distributed to targeted university students using a convenience sampling technique. A total of 300 useable questionnaires were analyzed using SmartPLS 4 software through partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the proposed research hypotheses. 

Findings-The study results revealed that GCP has a direct positive impact on both INST.T and SBA. The role of INST.T significantly mediates the relationship between GCP and SBA, while the moderating role of GN-Z EC significantly strengthens the path between INST.T and SBA. All five structural hypotheses were fully supported. 

Practical implications-This study highlights the crucial role of authentic green initiatives in building institutional trust and driving student advocacy in Pakistani universities. University leadership and marketing strategists must invest in visible green practices rather than superficial marketing. By aligning campus operations with the eco-values of Gen-Z students, institutions can foster long-term student loyalty and build organic brand equity. 

Originality/value-This study extends the green marketing literature in higher education by developing a unique moderated-mediation framework. It integrates Stakeholder Theory and Social Exchange Theory to explain how physical sustainability efforts convert into behavioral brand advocacy through psychological trust and generational boundary conditions.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the factors driving rural customers to engage in e-commerce, especially online buying, in the South Salmara Mankachar district of Assam, India. The district is predominantly rural and one of the most underdeveloped in the state, where the availability of organised retail stores is very limited. The study uses primary data collected from 120 respondents using a structured questionnaire, and basic statistical tools and exploratory factor analysis were employed to determine the key factors affecting consumers' adoption of ecommerce. Results indicate that perceived convenience is the most influential factor, especially in terms of time efficiency, home delivery and flexibility of payment. Other key considerations are perceived freedom and enjoyment, appealing pricing and deals, and product availability that is not easily found in local markets. The results also highlight the importance of social and informational factors such as customer reviews and ratings, recommendations by peers and social media, and transparent return and exchange policies in shaping the final purchase decision. In general, the study indicates that the rural customers are becoming more active participants in digital markets in a rational and value-driven way. Besides its contribution to the general literature of e-commerce, the study also offers useful insights to e-commerce firms and policymakers to tailor strategies that improve accessibility, trust and market penetration in the underserved rural areas.

title: Two Kinds of Nothing: What Insignificant Results in Finance Actually Show

detail.title: Two Kinds of Nothing: What Insignificant Results in Finance Actually Show

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No declaration of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was used for this study

detail.abstract: Claims of the form "we find no evidence that X affects Y" appear throughout the applied finance literature, yet whether such a claim contains evidence of absence or absence of evidence depends entirely on its confidence interval. Still, these intervals are rarely examined by authorsparticularly for insignificant results. The term "statistically insignificant" is routinely read to mean zero economic effect. However, a more honest description is that zero could not be rejected along with a range of other coefficient effect sizes. The crucial question is whether effect sizes in that range are consequential. This note distinguishes two kinds of insignificant results that are indistinguishable in a standard regression table: bounded null claims where the intervals reject effect sizes of consequence and thus represent a genuine finding, and vacuous null claims where even consequential effects-along with zero-remain unrejected and therefore establish nothing. The prevailing convention already takes a stand on the threshold for which effects matter: silently and arbitrarily, at wherever the interval's edges happen to fall. I propose a minimal reporting standard for regression results in applied finance, where the smallest consequential effect size is stated (in the units of the decision, per a named increment of the regressor) alongside the descriptive statistics and compared with the relevant edges of the confidence intervals of null claims. Using only the reported coefficient and standard error-and the proposed protocolauthors can distinguish bounded (informative) null claims that reject consequential effect sizes from vacuous null claims that establish no information, perhaps due to deficiencies in data or the identification strategy. The symmetric phrase "no effect" conceals, in particular, the frequent split verdict-bounded in one direction, vacuous in the other. In ongoing work, I apply this framework to published null claims in leading finance journals, beginning with my own.

title: The Politics of Vagueness: Strategic Ambiguity and the Democratic Accountability Paradox in Public Policy Communication

detail.title: The Politics of Vagueness: Strategic Ambiguity and the Democratic Accountability Paradox in Public Policy Communication

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am deeply interested in communication politics andx how words derive their persuasive power in politics
declarations.funderStatement: personal

detail.abstract: Political slogans often derive their persuasive power from ambiguity rather than precision. Campaign messages such as "Change" (Buhari, Nigeria, 2015), "Take Back Control" (United Kingdom), "Make America Great Again" (United States), and "Emi Lokan" (Tinubu, Nigeria, 2023) have mobilized broad coalitions despite offering few explicit policy commitments. While communication scholars have long acknowledged strategic ambiguity as a persuasive communication tool, insufficient attention has been paid to its implications for democratic accountability after elections. This paper argues that strategic ambiguity creates a Democratic Accountability Paradox. Ambiguous political messages increase electoral appeal by allowing multiple audiences to project their own expectations onto a campaign. However, the same flexibility complicates citizens' ability to assess whether elected officials have fulfilled their promises. Building on framing theory and recent scholarship in political communication, strategic rhetoric, policy framing, and audience interpretation, and drawing on post-election polling evidence from Nigeria and the United Kingdom, the paper develops an integrated account of how ambiguity functions as a political resource, how digital media intensify its effects, and what its limits are as an explanation for weak democratic accountability. Through comparative analysis of campaign slogans from Nigeria, the United Kingdom, and the United States, the paper demonstrates how ambiguity facilitates political mobilization while simultaneously undermining accountability mechanisms central to democratic systems.

detail.abstract: Persistent global trade imbalances, geopolitical fragmentation, and rising external-sector uncertainty have significantly reshaped India's trade environment during 2012-2026, creating new challenges for effective trade-policy design. This paper develops a quantitative dynamic equilibrium framework based on a multi-sector dynamic Ricardian model with endogenous international borrowing and lending to analyze optimal trade-policy responses under long-run external adjustment. The framework allows tariffs, trade distortions, and capital-control measures to evolve inter-temporally in response to productivity differentials, external imbalances, capital flows, and global macroeconomic shocks. Unlike conventional static trade models, it incorporates dynamic terms-of-trade effects and external-sector adjustment within a unified inter-temporal optimization framework. The model is calibrated using annual macroeconomic and international trade data from the World Bank, IMF, WTO, FRED, and RBI, covering major global disruptions such as the US-China trade war, the COVID-19 pandemic, and global supply-chain restructuring. Results indicate substantial time variation in India's optimal tradepolicy responses, with periods of heightened uncertainty requiring stronger policy intervention. Optimal policy reduces excessive trade exposure, improves externalsector stability, and enhances welfare through strategic tariff adjustments and calibrated capital-control measures, emphasizing the importance of dynamic trade management in an increasingly fragmented global economy.

title: The First-Rung Problem: AI, Labor, and the Coming Precariat
affiliations: The Digital Economist, The Digital Economist, The Digital Economist and The Digital Economist

detail.title: The First-Rung Problem: AI, Labor, and the Coming Precariat

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no financial, personal, or professional relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

keywords: AI AND THE FUTURE OF WORK

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is transforming labor markets—but the most immediate disruption may not appear as mass unemployment. Instead, the first signs are emerging through entry-level hiring compression, shifting task structures, and narrowing pathways into skilled careers. This policy paper examines how AI-driven changes in the nature of work could produce a “missing cohort” of early-career professionals and contribute to the formation of an AI precariat—workers structurally excluded from AI-enabled prosperity despite continued economic growth.

Drawing on emerging labor-market data, sectoral analysis, and cross-country sentiment indicators, the paper introduces the AI Anxiety Index, a comparative early-warning tool designed to identify where technological disruption may translate into social anxiety and institutional strain. It argues that the central policy challenge is not simply managing automation, but preserving career mobility, institutional trust, and inclusive access to opportunity during the AI transition.

The paper concludes with a set of enforceable policy recommendations, including AI Labor Impact Statements, career-ladder preservation mechanisms, transition-ready safety nets, and international cooperation through a Global AI Workforce Compact. Together, these proposals outline a governance agenda aimed at aligning AI-driven productivity gains with social stability, workforce resilience, and long-term economic competitiveness.

title: Women's Commuting After Childbirth: Evidence from U.S. Panel Data
affiliations: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.title: Women's Commuting After Childbirth: Evidence from U.S. Panel Data
detail.abstract: Post-childbirth commute burden is a potential source for labor market disparity between men and women. Recent work has documented substantial divergence of post-childbirth commuting distance between mothers and fathers in Norway. Using data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics that cover two distinct periods: 1970--1986 and 2011--2019, we find that U.S. mothers exit the labor force at substantially higher rates than fathers following childbirth, but mothers remaining employed show little change in commuting time or distance relative to their pre-birth patterns or to fathers. These contrasting patterns call for more cross-country research on post-childbirth commute changes.

title: Where the American Worker is being Squeezed

detail.title: Where the American Worker is being Squeezed

detail.abstract: This paper examines the earnings and housing position of full-time American workers across 19 major metropolitan areas, using U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics wage data, Census Bureau income and population figures, Zillow rent and home-value data, and the Harvard Joint Center for Housing Studies' cost-burden estimates. The median full-time worker earned $65,052 annualized in the second quarter of 2026, while the 25th-percentile worker earned only $44,200 — a range that places most of the lower half of the full-time workforce within an income band that is ordinary rather than exceptional. The 19 metropolitan areas analyzed contain approximately 35 percent of the U.S. population, situating the analysis within the dominant national settlement and labor-market pattern rather than a set of unusually expensive outliers. At $50,000 in annual income, typical asking rent alone consumes between 36 and 79 percent of gross earnings across the metros studied, before taxes, food, transportation, healthcare, or debt. Median household income has risen modestly above its 1976 CPI-equivalent level, but median new-home value relative to household income has risen from roughly 3.5x to 4.4x over the same period, and housing and transportation now account for just over half of average consumer spending. The paper argues that the central affordability problem is not that wages have failed to keep pace with inflation, but that a widening share of ordinary full-time workers face a geographic and distributional squeeze between typical earnings and the cost of secure housing — a gap concentrated in the labor markets where most Americans actually live and work.

detail.abstract: We study a matrix autoregressive (MAR) model whose coefficients are matrix analytic functions of network weight matrices. Our approach uses Frobenius covariants to reduce the parameter count from n^2+m^2 to n+m while allowing for spillovers through the network. Our estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal. Using monthly bilateral exports among 20 economies and a geographic-distance network, we find that 58% of exporter-side and 34% of importer-side spillover coefficients are statistically different from zero. Impulse responses to a single-pair shock and a regional-integration shock reveal significant spillovers on third economies, although these effects are an order of magnitude smaller than the direct effects.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes how the Bank of Canada responds to demand-driven versus supply-driven inflation. Using the decomposition method of Shapiro (2024), Canadian headline inflation is divided into demand and supply components and incorporated into a Taylor Rule. The results show a larger point estimate for demand-driven inflation with a coefficient of 0.161, compared with a corresponding supply-driven inflation estimate of 0.132. To explain this difference, Phillips curves are estimated for each component, with the results being consistent with comparatively more anchored inflation expectations during supply-driven episodes, which may help explain the more muted policy response. Formal coefficient-equality tests indicate that these differences are estimated imprecisely, while local-projection results provide complementary evidence of a clearer and more persistent response of demand-driven inflation to monetary tightening. The small gap between the coefficients may partly reflect the Bank of Canada's inflation targeting framework and the use of headline inflation, which includes volatile, largely supply-driven components.

publicationDetails.journalName: DFG Center for Advanced Studies - Foundations of Law & Finance (LawFin) Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: The global adoption of IFRS 9 requires banks to recognize loan loss provisions based on forward-looking credit loss estimates. While these rules enhance the timeliness of loss recognition, they also expand the scope for managerial discretion in loss estimation. Using supervisory data on German banks' internal rating models, we examine how banks respond to these countervailing incentives. Relative to unaffected banks, IFRS 9 adopters update their internal credit risk estimates more frequently, consistent with a general improvement in the timeliness of loss recognition, yet assign systematically more favorable internal ratings to otherwise identical borrowers. A lower precision of these ratings accompanies this pattern, consistent with the strategic use of increased reporting discretion outweighing the greater timeliness of the estimates. The implications for bank lending are twofold. First, to counter the increased cost of high-risk lending, banks curtail credit to borrowers most likely to experience internal rating downgrades that would trigger additional provisioning in future periods, with these lending changes extending broadly across the non-investment-grade segment and indicating a general portfolio shift toward lower credit risk. Second, lending changes cluster around seemingly arbitrary provisioning thresholds where expected credit losses are systematically underreported, suggesting that expanded reporting discretion distorts lending in a way that optimizes model input rather than portfolio risk.

title: Finite-frequency Reciprocal Travel-Time Signal Processing for Aeroacoustic Source Localization under Moving-medium Bias
affiliations: Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST), Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST), Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST), Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST) and Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology (GIST)

detail.title: Finite-frequency Reciprocal Travel-Time Signal Processing for Aeroacoustic Source Localization under Moving-medium Bias
detail.abstract: Acoustic source localization in mechanical and aerospace systems often uses signal models that assume a known quiescent propagation medium. Open-jet shear layers, wakes, duct flows, and lined-wall conditions violate this assumption by biasing phase, waveform, and cross-correlation time-delay features before beamforming or source fitting. This paper develops a physics-based finite-frequency reciprocal time-delay processing framework for estimating and correcting such moving-medium bias. Born sensitivity kernels map wave-speed, density/impedance-like, and mean-flow perturbations to timing residuals, while source--receiver reversal forms reciprocal-even and reciprocal-odd channels. Thermodynamic perturbations are even in the reference model, vortical advection is predominantly odd, and compressible-flow leakage enters the even channel through a divergence term. Bayesian regularization, resolution diagnostics, and D-optimal pair selection quantify uncertainty, cross-talk, and calibration-pair value. Analytic Helmholtz benchmarks validate the parity predictions, broadband wave-packet calculations recover the finite-frequency-to-ray trend, and discrete linearized-Euler/adjoint tests verify solver-level volume and wall sensitivities. Open-jet tests compare homogeneous steering, fitted parametric shear-layer correction, ray-based field correction, finite-bandwidth field correction, and a true-medium lower bound. In an illustrative noisy synthetic open-jet test, the finite-bandwidth field correction reduces median localization bias by about 98.8\% relative to homogeneous steering, while a correctly specified parametric correction is nearly noise limited. A nonparallel mismatch test and an off-ray anomaly benchmark show when field-based and finite-bandwidth processing provide advantages over fixed parametric or ray-delay models.

detail.abstract: Older workers' health can fail in two ways: gradually, as deficits accumulate into frailty, or suddenly, with a first diagnosis of stroke, heart disease, or cancer. Using four waves of a national Chinese panel of people aged 45 and older, I estimate the labor-supply response to both, in the same data with the same research design. A sudden diagnosis cuts labor-force participation by 6.7 percentage points, a tenth of the participation rate. A gradual decline that moves measured health nearly twice as far leaves participation essentially unchanged: declines beyond 2.5 percentage points are ruled out, and the gap between the two responses is itself precisely estimated. Gradual decline instead shows up, suggestively, as a work-year about five percent shorter. What ties health to work here is the capacity to perform everyday tasks, not diagnoses or mood. Programs triggered by discrete health events will miss workers who decline gradually and keep working.

detail.abstract: Purpose-Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly operates both as an ESG-enabling capability and as an ESG exposure in its own right. This article examines how corporate AI affects sustainability measurement, environmental performance, workforce outcomes, information governance, internal controls, board accountability and disclosure credibility. Design/ methodology/approach: The study employs a structured integrative evidence synthesis. It consolidates the evidence base in the author's 2026 working paper. It updates it through targeted validation of recent peer-reviewed empirical studies, systematic and bibliometric reviews, and official sources from the International Energy Agency, United Nations Environment Programme, World Economic Forum, NIST, OECD, IFRS Foundation, Securities and Exchange Board of India and European Union. Evidence is coded across six domains: ESG measurement and reporting, environmental footprint, social and workforce impact, governance and model risk, supply-chain due diligence, and regulatory/assurance implications. Findings-The literature supports a conditional dual effect. AI can improve ESG data extraction, green innovation, information governance, anomaly detection, climate risk analysis, and internal control quality. Yet the same systems can generate material environmental and governance liabilities through electricity and water demand, opaque or biased models, hallucination, cybersecurity and privacy exposure, vendor dependence, workforce disruption and uncertain responsibility. The most important unresolved issue is therefore not whether AI can support ESG, but whether firms can produce an auditable chain of evidence demonstrating that AI-supported ESG decisions and disclosures are reliable, lawful and accountable. detail.abstract: This article examines how agro-pastoral innovation affects food insecurity among Cameroonian households, with particular attention to the mediating role of resilience. Drawing on innovation diffusion theory, the capability approach, and the livelihood resilience framework, the study proposes an analytical framework in which agro-pastoral innovation affects food insecurity both directly and indirectly, through the strengthening of households' resilience capacities. The empirical strategy relies on an autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) model with an error correction mechanism, complemented by a mediation analysis following the approaches of Baron and Kenny (1986) and Preacher and Hayes (2008), with bootstrapped indirect effects. The article details the full econometric specification, the required diagnostic tests, and the testable hypotheses, and discusses the expected implications for food security and rural innovation policy in Cameroon.

title: The Impact of Fiscal Policy to Promote Healthy Diets: Evidence from the Navajo Nation
affiliations: Syracuse University,  and Indiana University

detail.title: The Impact of Fiscal Policy to Promote Healthy Diets: Evidence from the Navajo Nation
detail.abstract:
One of the most comprehensive fiscal policies to improve diet was adopted by the Navajo Nation; the Healthy Diné Nation Act (HDNA) of 2014-15 consists of two parts: 1) an exemption from sales tax for healthy foods and beverages; and 2) a tax increase on unhealthy foods and beverages. Together, they create a price wedge of 7-8% between healthy and unhealthy foods. We estimate difference-in-difference models and event studies that estimate the effect of the HDNA on a variety of health conditions relating to diet and weight for newborns and mothers which are recorded in birth certificate data. We find no evidence that the HDNA improved these outcomes; our estimates are precise enough to rule out improvements in gestational diabetes as large as those reported for U.S. city SSB taxes. Possible explanations for the null results include incomplete retailer implementation and cross-border shopping.

title: Where the CHIPS Fall: Local Labor Market Impacts of Semiconductor Mega-Investments in Maricopa County, Arizona
affiliations: Federal Reserve Bank of Boston and Federal Reserve Bank of Boston

detail.title: Where the CHIPS Fall: Local Labor Market Impacts of Semiconductor Mega-Investments in Maricopa County, Arizona
detail.abstract: This paper examines the local labor market effects of mega-scale semiconductor investment, using Maricopa County, Arizona, as a case study. The county has received about $300 billion in commitments through the 2030s under the CHIPS and Science Act of 2022, the largest placebased industrial investment in recent US history. Using synthetic difference-indifferences , we find large employment gains, but few of these gains occur within the manufacturing sector. Semiconductor manufacturing shows no measurable net change, as hiring at new facilities offsets reductions at existing ones. The gains instead concentrate in construction—13 to 33 percent above the synthetic counterfactual—and in supply chain sectors—5 to 46 percent above—which together represent about 9,700 and 7,100 jobs, respectively. More than 80 percent of the latter fall into wholesale trade and technical services rather than manufacturing. We attribute this composition to the high capital-to-labor ratio of semiconductor fabrication and to a scale threshold in supplier relocation.

title: CentaurBench: Benchmarking LLM Capabilities on Augmenting vs. Automating Real-World Work Tasks
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley, University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: CentaurBench: Benchmarking LLM Capabilities on Augmenting vs. Automating Real-World Work Tasks
detail.abstract:
Most LLM benchmarks rank models on their ability to automate work tasks. In practice, however, models are often used to assist other (human or LLM) agents. The question that drives model selection is therefore not only which model produces the best output, but which model most improves the work of another (weaker) agent. We introduce a unified framework that evaluates the capability of models to automate and augment another agent's performance. Across seven economically grounded real-world tasks, an assistant model writes assistance text for a standardized lower-capacity worker model, which produces the deliverable. In automation mode, the assistant produces the output directly. Outputs are scored through blind pairwise comparisons by an LLM judge panel with task-specific rubrics, replicated across ten runs. Rankings across the two regimes are only modestly correlated, and the automation winner loses augmentation on five of seven tasks. Assistance is not reliably positive. The unaided worker outranks every assisted condition on three tasks, and only one model's guidance beats no guidance on average. These results suggest that automation ability is an incomplete proxy for assistance quality, motivating benchmarks that evaluate models according to the roles they play in human-AI and multi-agent systems.

title: Democratizing Private Markets: Equilibrium Predictions
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business, University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Democratizing Private Markets: Equilibrium Predictions
detail.abstract:
We study how opening private markets to retail investors affects investors and firms. Calibrating a production-based asset-pricing model, we find that democratization raises retail investors' welfare, but barely. Retail investors benefit little from democratization even if they face no extra cost or other disadvantage relative to institutional investors. The private market is simply too small for improved risk sharing to matter much. Whether or not private-market retail investing is costly, democratization substantially reshapes private firms' ownership and materially reduces their cost of capital, leading them to grow. Private equity earns a positive CAPM alpha, which shrinks after democratization.

title: Rising Income Risk at the Top
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison - Department of Economics, University of Minnesota - Minneapolis, New York University (NYU) - New York University, Carnegie Mellon University, U.S. Census Bureau, Social, Economic, and Housing Statistics Division and University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - University of California, San Diego

detail.title: Rising Income Risk at the Top
detail.abstract:
We document an increase in U.S. income risk from 1969 to 2019 using newly digitized IRS tax returns, distinguishing permanent from transitory risk. Since the 1970s, permanent income risk increased across the distribution, but most sharply among high earners, rising nearly 70% among the top 5%. We show that, even among top earners, large negative income shocks strongly predict financial distress and higher income risk is linked with higher savings. In a quantitative life-cycle model, rising income risk concentrated at the top lowers the risk-free rate by 0.7pp, increases wealth inequality, and contributes to the "savings glut of the rich."

title: Making Everyone’s Preferences Count: A Prospect Theory Approach to Valuing Health Improvements
affiliations: University of Southern California, University of Southern California, University of Southern California and University of Southern California - Schaeffer Center for Health Policy  and Economics

detail.title: Making Everyone’s Preferences Count: A Prospect Theory Approach to Valuing Health Improvements
detail.abstract:
Health technology assessment bodies and policymakers have grappled with the issue of whose preferences – the general healthy population or the patient population – should be incorporated into traditional cost-effectiveness analysis. This debate arises because healthy individuals and patients often value the same health state differently, and cost-effectiveness will undervalue health-related quality of life (HRQoL) for individuals with chronic illness or disability because it cannot account for adaptation. Prospect theory (PT) provides a framework that permits adaptation since it assumes individuals evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point. We estimate utility over HRQoL in a PT framework in a nationally representative U.S. population and compare directly with utility estimates in an EU framework from the same population. Consistent with previous studies in the monetary and health domains, we find evidence of probability weighting bias and loss aversion over health. Using the PT utility estimates, we demonstrate how PT can be incorporated into healthcare value assessment and present the resulting implications for medical decision making.

title: Fool's Gold? How the USD lost its Shine
affiliations: , Banque de France and Banque de France

detail.title: Fool's Gold? How the USD lost its Shine
detail.abstract:
This paper investigates the determinants of international investors’ portfolio choices between gold and sovereign bonds in an environment shaped by economic and geopolitical shocks. We develop an endogenous portfolio choice model where reserve safety has a political dimension — sovereign bonds issued by the dominant reserve country are more liquid but exposed to the issuer’s sanctions authority, while gold offers sanctions protection at the cost of lower liquidity. Our model implies that US convenience yields fall during periods of high sanction risk, as safe-asset demand fragments along geopolitical lines. Empirically, periods of elevated geopolitical risk coincide with higher gold prices and 10-year Treasury yields. In such periods, the average composition of official reserves shifts toward gold, with countries less aligned with the US increasing their holdings to a greater extent.

title: Labor Mobility and the Level of Unemployment in a Currency Union
affiliations: U.S. International Trade Commission, University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Department of Economics, KU Leuven and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Department of Economics

detail.title: Labor Mobility and the Level of Unemployment in a Currency Union
detail.abstract:
Unemployment rates are substantially higher and more volatile in the euro area relative to the United States. We ask to what extent the lack of cross-country labor mobility can account for unemployment dynamics in Europe. Our analytical model incorporates downward nominal wage rigidity and an endogenous migration decision. Firms are unable to freely adjust wages during economic contractions, generating an asymmetric distribution of unemployment over the business cycle. The model is calibrated to the dynamics of unemployment and net migration in a typical euro area country. An increase in labor mobility to that observed in the United States and holding all other parameters fixed would reduce the volatility of euro area unemployment by 28% and return over 1,000,000 unemployed to the workforce. The welfare cost to a typical euro area country of the currency union is 4.1 percent of permanent consumption; increasing labor mobility reduces this cost to about 3.55 percent.

title: A Theory of International Official Lending
affiliations: Tsinghua University - School of Economics & Management, Tsinghua University and Emory University

detail.title: A Theory of International Official Lending
detail.abstract:
Official lending is large, senior, and countercyclical, continuing after sovereigns fall into arrears on private debt. We ask why sovereign finance exhibits this division of labor across creditors. In a production economy where a risk-averse sovereign privately allocates imported inputs, commitment is limited on both sides, and monitoring generates a noisy signal, the constrained-optimal allocation is decentralized by defaultable private debt, senior non-defaultable multilateral debt, and concessional bilateral debt whose relief is tied to the signal. Production remains distorted, but the sovereign is never excluded: official lending is monitored liquidity provision. A calibration reproduces procyclical private and countercyclical official debt.

title: Kumon Up: Private Tutoring Centers and Student Achievement
affiliations: and

detail.title: Kumon Up: Private Tutoring Centers and Student Achievement
detail.abstract:
Private tutoring chains like Kumon and Sylvan have expanded rapidly in recent decades. Combining data on business locations, household spending, and district test scores, we study who uses these centers and how they affect academic skills. Nearly half of tutoring users are from the top income decile, with Asian and White households five and two times as likely to purchase tutoring as Black and Hispanic households. A staggered differences-in-differences design shows the opening of a district's first chain center raises district-wide math and reading scores by 0.02-0.03 standard deviations, at a much lower cost than public spending typically producing similar gains. Math effects are largest for White and Asian students, so that center entry widens racial achievement gaps, though less so in more racially integrated districts. These private investments help their users, deepen educational inequality, and shape outcomes by which state accountability systems and families judge schools.

title: Modular Gait Control based on Machine Learning and Predicted Step Viability
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Modular Gait Control based on Machine Learning and Predicted Step Viability

keywords.keywords: Trajectory planninggait stabilitymachine learning deep learningmultilayer perceptron robotic locomotion.

detail.abstract: Robot locomotion relies on real-time decision-making to preserve stability and ensure continuous movement even in the presence of disturbances. In this work, we present a modular machine learning (ML)–based framework by developing methods to apply the Predicted Step Viability (PSV) algorithm in real-time to generate suboptimal gaits for a bipedal robot. PSV is an optimal stability criterion and trajectory planning algorithm that uses the complete robot model to solve a multi-stage optimization problem, ensuring not only the optimal current step but also the existence and stability of future steps. Due to its computational complexity, PSV cannot be used in real-time control. We address the leg trajectory planning problem by introducing three interconnected ML models: (i) a multilayer perceptron estimates the probability that a configuration is recoverable, optimized under physical constraints, which is used to find the most stable configuration that can be reached at the end of the step; (ii) a bidirectional long short‑term memory (LSTM) network predicts the step duration from partial time-series observations; and (iii) another LSTM predicts the control trajectory required to execute a step, conditioned on start and target configurations and the predicted duration. Simulations on a planar, five‑segment bipedal robot demonstrate high predictive accuracy and the ability to generate dynamically feasible trajectories that ensure stability in real-time. Compared with baseline PSV control simulated without real-time constraints, the proposed ML framework provides real-time embeddable, modular, and versatile trajectory planning and stability assessment modules that can be applied to different bipedal robots.

title: Explaining the Predictive Performance of Police in Cases of Domestic Abuse
affiliations: University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy, Washington University in St. Louis and London School of Economics - Centre for Economic Performance

detail.title: Explaining the Predictive Performance of Police in Cases of Domestic Abuse
detail.abstract:
Police in England and Wales are asked to predict the likelihood of serious recidivism in domestic abuse cases, with little support beyond a flawed questionnaire. To analyze their decisions, we first develop methods to deal with a censoring problem that arises because the officer’s prediction may change the outcome she was attempting to predict. Even after adjusting for censoring, we find predictive performance to be low, even lower in some cases than what one would expect by chance. We next ask whether their predictions represent mistakes, and provide several types of confirmatory evidence. We ask how officers formulate their predictions, and we find evidence consistent with representativeness bias, overreaction, and categorization and selective attention. We find that higher-skill officers use information not captured by the questionnaire to improve their predictions, whereas lower-skill officers use such information in ways that reduce accuracy.

title: The Great American Property Tax Freak Out
affiliations: Yale University - Law School

detail.title: The Great American Property Tax Freak Out

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
There has been a lot of news over the last two years, so it is understandable that neither the mass media nor the legal academy has focused on what is happening with the steady mainstay of local government finance, the property tax. While attention was elsewhere, though, the property tax has gone through a revolution, one nearly as profound as the great property tax revolt of the late 1970s and 80s that led to profound changes like California’s Proposition 13 and Massachusetts’s Proposition 2 1/2. In the last three years, a number of states have substantially reformed their property tax systems, providing huge tax benefits to owner-occupied homes and shifting the burden of paying for services like schools and police to commercial property owners (including rental apartment buildings), to other local taxes, and to state funding, which itself largely comes from sources like sales taxes and income taxes. A few, including Florida, Ohio, North Dakota, and Texas, have considered going further, either completely abandoning property taxation for owner-occupied housing or even abandoning property taxation entirely. 

This Essay tries to explain why we have seen such radical changes in property tax systems around the country. It argues that, just as with the property tax revolt of the 1970s, the driving force was rising property values and our homeowner-dominated state and local politics. One might think that homeowners would be happy that their largest asset has appreciated substantially in value, as homes did, particularly in suburbs, in the post-COVID period. But because property taxes are wealth taxes, property owners have responded to their increasing wealth with political anger, pushing shifts in property tax policy, often leading to increasing rates on commercial property owners who have seen declining values during the same period.

More importantly, the Essay seeks to establish the policy implications of these radical transformations in property taxes. It argues that these reforms shift the property tax from a tool homeowners use collectively to provide for locally-wanted services towards a more standard form of redistributive taxation, charging commercial property owners to pay for services for homeowners. Further, they will lead to greater state authority over local governments, less stable funding for local governments (but also less tax foreclosure in recessions), and stricter zoning controls (but more building of homes where it is legal). Perhaps most notably, these property tax reforms will lead to higher housing costs, and thus constitute a substantial transfer of wealth towards people who already own homes and have already seen their net worth increase substantially in the post-COVID housing market.

title: This Time Is (Mostly) Different: U.S. Tightening Cycles and Global Resilience in the 1980s vs 2020s
affiliations: University of California, Santa Cruz, University of California, Santa Cruz and Vassar College

detail.title: This Time Is (Mostly) Different: U.S. Tightening Cycles and Global Resilience in the 1980s vs 2020s
detail.abstract:
Post-pandemic inflation raised fears that U.S. monetary tightening would trigger a repeat of the 1982 sudden stop in capital flows to emerging economies. Yet as of 2026 no global recession has followed. We establish three stylized facts distinguishing the 1980s from the 2020s, beyond the shift to flexible exchange rates: monetary policy effectiveness, fiscal space, and external vulnerabilities. We rationalize them in a Mundell-Fleming framework with a fiscal space constraint, which predicts a central role for fiscal space in transmitting foreign currency risk-free rate increases. Cross-country evidence confirms that fiscal space shapes economic performance post-tightening.

title: The Distribution and Consequences of Natural Disasters: Evidence from U.S. Wildfire Victims
affiliations: University of British Columbia (UBC), University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics, University of Virginia and U.S. Census Bureau

detail.title: The Distribution and Consequences of Natural Disasters: Evidence from U.S. Wildfire Victims
detail.abstract:
The economic burden of natural disasters is shaped by who is exposed, who experiences losses, how those losses alter individual economic trajectories, and how affected communities evolve in the aftermath. We link property-level damage data from over 100 U.S. wildfires to administrative tax and Census data to understand individual-level relationships between disaster damage and economic outcomes. Residents of burned areas are wealthier than the U.S. population on average, but within these wildfire perimeters the likelihood that a home burns is negatively correlated with pre-fire income. Home destruction imposes costs beyond rebuilding the property: occupants of destroyed homes experience lower income for three years post-fire, producing cumulative income losses equal to 26 percent of pre-fire annual income. We do not detect income or employment effects for residents without direct property damage. Community recovery is slow and accompanied by changes in composition. Four years after a fire, half of destroyed addresses remain unoccupied and reoccupied addresses house residents with substantially higher incomes than before.

title: Can We Build More Effective Place-Based Policies? Theory and Evidence
affiliations: University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics and University of California, Irvine - Department of Economics

detail.title: Can We Build More Effective Place-Based Policies? Theory and Evidence
detail.abstract:
Amid renewed policy interest, the academic literature on place-based programs has expanded dramatically in recent years. In this essay, we review recent theoretical and empirical work in an effort to assess when and why place-based job creation policies succeed or fail. Drawing on theory, we describe key dimensions on which place-based programs vary and discuss evidence on the consequences of different design choices. We conclude with several lessons for the next generation of place-based programs.

title: Firms as Electoral Monopsonies
affiliations: University of California, San Diego (UCSD), University of Alberta, Indiana University - Kelley School of Business - Department of Finance and Indiana University - Kelley School of Business

detail.title: Firms as Electoral Monopsonies
detail.abstract:
We study how dominant employers can act as *electoral monopsonies*, using local labor market power to shape political preferences and electoral outcomes. We first present original survey evidence showing that workers at major local employers are more likely to experience employer political communication and to report that their employers influence their voting behavior and career expectations. We then develop a model in which a dominant employer can affect voters’ preferences by shaping their expectations about how wages and employment depend on electoral outcomes. We distinguish a passive channel, through which workers internalize firms’ economic interests, from an active channel, through which dominant employers strategically influence these expectations. Under the active channel, labor market power translates into political power and can generate political failures by inducing voters to oppose policies they would otherwise support. The model also shows how electoral monopsonies can contribute to political polarization, constrain political platforms, and substitute for campaign spending. Using U.S. individual-level voting data and a shift-share design based on national industry concentration shocks and predetermined local employment shares, we show that greater electoral monopsony power increases Republican voter turnout. Counterfactual estimates imply that reducing electoral monopsony power could have narrowly changed the outcomes of the 2016 and 2024 presidential elections.

title: What Work Does Generative AI Do?
affiliations: , Vanderbilt University, Academic Dean, Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) and Vanderbilt University

detail.title: What Work Does Generative AI Do?
detail.abstract:
We measure how workers use genAI for their jobs in a nationally representative survey linking genAI adoption to detailed occupations and tasks. Our data provide the first task-level genAI adoption indexes, which we show can inform analyses of genAI’s labor market impact. Exposure scores explain some, but far from all, of the variation in adoption across occupations and tasks. We also distinguish our indexes from measures based on genAI platform chat logs, which differ conceptually and tend to over-classify chats into generic activities spanning many occupations. Finally, we highlight that current adoption is widespread but shallow: genAI is used across many occupations and tasks, yet within most of them, fewer than half of workers adopt. This indicates substantial variation among workers doing very similar work, suggesting that understanding who adopts may matter as much as understanding which tasks genAI assists.

detail.title: Finances of the Nation Minimum Wage In Canada—How Has The Financial Situation Of Households Changed Over The Past 10 Years?

detail.abstract: For almost 60 years, the Canadian Tax Foundation published an annual monograph, Finances of the Nation, and its predecessor, The National Finances. In a change of format, the 2014 Canadian Tax Journal introduced a new “Finances of the Nation” feature, which presents annual surveys of provincial and territorial budgets and topical articles on taxation and public expenditures in Canada. The minimum wage still generates heated debate in Canada, even though it is earned by only a small share of the workforce. This article compares the financial situation of four types of households earning the minimum wage over time (between 2015 and 2025) and across provinces. It argues that the comparison cannot be based solely on wages. The broader context needs to be taken into account, including the tax system, benefits offered, and the cost of living. Under this broad view, the real disposable income of households has increased over the 10-year period, in all provinces and for each type of household. The rate of coverage of basic needs has also seen across-the-board increases, but the extent of these increases varies by province and type of household. The underlying data for the Finances of the Nation monographs and for the articles in this journal will be published online in the near future.

title: Smart Contracting in Network Markets
affiliations: Stanford University - Graduate School of Business and University of Pennsylvania - The Wharton School

detail.title: Smart Contracting in Network Markets
detail.abstract:
With complete-information bilateral bargaining in network settings, holdup is eliminated when contracts across the network are agreed atomically (all or none) via a smart contract. Applications include over-the-counter asset trading, third-party-financed purchase agreements, and land assembly. Under a novel extensive-form bargaining protocol, a firm can give a “greenlight” to the terms of a contract proposed to that firm, and the protocol automatically converts those terms into a binding contract if the terms proposed to all other firms are likewise given greenlights. In any Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium with Markov strategies, firms immediately agree on socially efficient contracts.
