detail.title: A Competitive World

publicationDetails.detailsText: NHH Dept. of Economics Discussion Paper No. 11/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Norwegian School of Economics, Department of Economics Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We provide globally representative evidence on two attitudes toward competition: individuals' willingness to compete and the importance they attach to boys and girls being willing to compete, using a novel survey module that we fielded as part of the 2022 Gallup World Poll. The data cover more than 66,000 individuals across 62 countries. Men are more willing to compete than women in all but two countries, and willingness to compete is higher among younger, more educated, and higher-income individuals. Attitudes toward children's willingness to compete vary substantially across countries, with competitiveness valued more for boys in some countries and for girls in others. Both attitudes are systematically related to the economic and social environment. Individuals exposed to greater inequality or faster population growth during their formative years are more willing to compete and place greater importance on children being willing to compete. Greater exposure to gender equality during formative years is associated with smaller gender gaps in both adults' willingness to compete and attitudes toward the competitiveness of boys and girls. Our findings reveal striking global regularities while highlighting the role of the social environment in shaping attitudes toward competition.

title: Unexpected Outcomes of Vice Regulation: Pornography Laws, Supplier Exit, and Rape
affiliations: University of Arizona, San Diego State University and

detail.title: Unexpected Outcomes of Vice Regulation: Pornography Laws, Supplier Exit, and Rape

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Vice-good regulation is often designed to reduce harm by restricting access. Yet such restrictions may reorganize markets and behavior in ways that generate unintended spillovers. We examine this possibility in the context of online pornography. Beginning in 2023, 21 U.S. states implemented age-verification laws intended to protect minors from exposure to adult sexual content. In practice, these laws increased the effort and privacy costs of access for adults and prompted a major pornography platform to withdraw from states adopting the laws, creating a substantial restriction on product access. Using FBI crime data from 2,052 counties between 2022 and 2025, we exploit staggered policy implementation in a staggered difference-indifferences design, estimating counterfactual outcomes using partially pooled synthetic controls. We find that restricting access to the pornography market caused an increase in rape offenses recorded by law enforcement: during the first 12 months after implementation, incidents of rape were 2.5% higher in restricted counties than in their synthetic counterparts. This result is stable across alternative estimators, samples, time horizons, outcome measures, inference procedures, policy-confound exclusions, and placebo tests. The policy also increased juvenile-perpetrated rape, even though minors were the intended beneficiaries of the regulation. The findings show that policy-induced market reorganization for vice goods can trigger unintended behavioral responses with alarming welfare consequences.

title: Does the Haryana State Education Budget Translate to Learning Outcomes? A District-Level Analysis

detail.title: Does the Haryana State Education Budget Translate to Learning Outcomes? A District-Level Analysis

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study relies exclusively on secondary analysis of publicly available, fully anonymized, district-level data datasets (ASER, PARAKH, PGI-D, and UDISE+). As it involves no primary data collection or human subjects interaction, formal Institutional Review Board (IRB) or ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant or funding from public, commercial, or non-profit sector agencies. The paper was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Haryana invests a significant amount of money in education and, by one widely-read measure, has experienced one of the largest post-pandemic learning recoveries in the country. By another, equally official measure, it has dropped from eighth to fourteenth nationally among state school systems-and sits below the national average for what a Class 3 child actually knows. This paper holds those two facts in the same hand. It asks a seemingly simple question: when the state writes a large cheque for education, do children in its districts learn more? It answers using data drawn from household and school surveys-the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER 2024) and the PARAKH Rashtriya Sarvekshan 2024-together with the Performance Grading Index for Districts (PGI-D 2024-25) and the UDISE+ data system. In short, the answer is "not reliably, and not evenly." Across Haryana, district school-system scores range, on a 600-point scale, from about 377 points (Gurugram and Panchkula near the top) down to Nuh, the lowest at 275 points. Purchasing inputs (buildings, toilets, STEM laboratories, books) is a far more predictable use of spending than purchasing results (a child reading a story or doing division). The paper sets out a simple "leaky-pipe" model linking spending to learning, presents an econometric specification ready for the day district-level expenditure data is published, and argues that what determines whether rupees become learning is not the rupees themselves but the machinery of the pipewhen funds are spent, how teachers are deployed, and how each district is governed.

title: Semantic Alignment, Chronological Distance, and Citation-Network Prominence in Citation Formation: Evidence from Ten Citation Corpora

detail.title: Semantic Alignment, Chronological Distance, and Citation-Network Prominence in Citation Formation: Evidence from Ten Citation Corpora

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Competing interests: The author has no competing interests to declare.
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: Funding: No funding was received for conducting this study.

detail.abstract: What survives after temporal leakage is rigorously removed from citation link prediction? This paper answers that question across ten large-scale bibliographic corpora. We introduce a strongly leakage-mitigated methodological framework in which all network-derived quantities are computed exclusively from information available prior to the publication year of the citing paper. We formalize four forms of temporal leakage-future citation leakage, future topology leakage, metadata leakage, and semantic leakage-and apply this framework to ten bibliographic datasets retrieved from Dimensions.ai, spanning five broad scholarly domains: Science (Protein Folding, CRISPR), Engineering (Additive Manufacturing, Corrosion Protection), BioMed (Neuroblastoma, Osteosarcoma), Social Science (Income Inequality, Organizational Behavior), and Humanities (Film Studies, Memory Studies). Each corpus covers the period 1975-2024. The goal of this study is not to maximize citation prediction accuracy, but to decompose citation formation into distinct explanatory components under temporally rigorous conditions. Gradient Boosting achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.530 to 0.734 under temporally rigorous evaluation; these scores reflect the intrinsic difficulty of the prediction task under strict leakage-mitigated conditions, not a failure of the predictive model. We decompose citation formation into three components: semantic alignment (S), chronological distance (T), and citation-network prominence factors (N prom). Under this decomposition, chronological recency (T) dominates prediction across almost all corpora. Once the candidate set is restricted to plausible contemporaneous papers from the same topical corpus, directional semantic alignment adds little discriminative power beyond chronological recency: in four of the ten corpora, cited papers exhibit marginally lower directional semantic alignment to the citing paper than non-cited candidates. When citations occur despite weak semantic alignment, they tend to be temporally proximate, though they do not exhibit a consistent prominence pattern. We conclude that under leakage-controlled conditions, citation formation exhibits substantial domain-specific heterogeneity, but chronological distance factors consistently contribute more predictive signal than directional semantic alignment or citation-network prominence factors.

reference: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 213
title: Artificial Intelligence in Wealth Management: Fiduciary Responsibility and Regulatory Adaptation under EU Law
affiliations: Democritus University of Thrace, Law School

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence in Wealth Management: Fiduciary Responsibility and Regulatory Adaptation under EU Law

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Banking Institute Working Paper Series No. 213
publicationDetails.journalName: European Banking Institute (EBI) Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the wealth-management industry, accelerating its transition from a relationship-based and human-centred professional service to a technologically mediated, data-driven, autonomous form of financial intermediation. Historically grounded in fiduciary-like duties of loyalty, diligence, confidentiality, and acting in the client’s best interests, wealth management has evolved beyond its association with private banking into a holistic service encompassing portfolio management, investment advice, retirement planning, tax and estate planning. Robo-advisors, large language models, and agentic AI systems have democratised access to personalised financial services for retail investors, supporting financial inclusion and capital-market participation. Yet the substitution of human judgment by algorithms raises questions on the viability of the fiduciary paradigm underpinning these relationships.

This article examines the implications of AI deployment in wealth management through the lens of European Union law. It analyses the principal risks associated with AI-enabled advisory and portfolio-management activities, including opacity, explainability deficits, conflicts of interest, discriminatory outcomes, manipulative design, hallucinations, data-quality failures, and threats to market integrity and financial stability. Attention is devoted to the tension between the promises of scalability, efficiency, and personalisation offered by AI and the enduring objectives of investor protection and trust in financial markets.

Against this background, the article develops a layered interpretation of the European regulatory framework governing wealth-management AI. It analyses the interaction between sectoral legislation, particularly MiFID II, IDD, and DORA, and horizontal instruments, including the AI Act, GDPR, and the revised Product Liability Directive. The study identifies an apparent asymmetry between risk classification and fiduciary intensity, since most wealth-management AI systems are treated as limited-risk despite their potential to affect severely life savings, retirement outcomes, and market stability. It argues, however, that when interpreted teleologically and systematically, the combined operation of sectoral and cross-sectoral legislation produces a coherent framework of obligations for the AI systems providers and deployers, capable of addressing the distinctive risks posed by AI-enabled wealth management.

A central thesis advanced is that the European Supervisory Authorities (ESMA, EBA, EIOPA), play a decisive role in bridging the gap between technologically neutral statutory provisions and rapidly evolving AI applications. Through guidelines, opinions and other soft-law instruments, these authorities translate professional duties into concrete AI-governance expectations relating to transparency, explainability, documentation, data governance, human oversight, auditability, model validation and operational resilience. Fiduciary responsibility is therefore not displaced but operationalised through an increasingly sophisticated framework of technological governance and supervisory oversight.

The article further situates wealth-management AI within the evolving EU legislative landscape. Recent initiatives, including the CCD II, the DMD II, the Digital Omnibus reforms, and the RIS, reveal a broader regulatory movement towards enhanced rights to human involvement, meaningful explanation, protection against dark digital interfaces, and improved retail-investor empowerment, while also seeking to simplify disproportionate compliance obligations and preserve European competitiveness. Rather than signalling the tightening of regulatory regime for wealth-management AI, these developments point towards the incremental adaptation and refinement of existing legal frameworks.

Finally, the article highlights the challenges arising in non-harmonised components of wealth management, particularly tax advice and estate planning, both closely connected to legal advice. Unlike investment, banking, and insurance activities, these domains remain subject to national professional rules, raising questions regarding professional authorisation, accountability, and the scope of AI-assisted recommendation and decision-making. It is argued that AI systems operating in such contexts cannot lawfully substitute qualified professional judgment and should incorporate effective technical guardrails and human intervention mechanisms to reduce liability risks. The article concludes that AI can be accommodated within the fiduciary architecture of wealth management only through robust governance, proportionate systems-quality management, widespread explainability, effective human oversight, supervisory coordination, and strengthened financial and AI literacy among all relevant stakeholders.

title: The Cult of the Median. From the Illusion of Middle Values to the Architecture of the Real Market
affiliations: and Independent

detail.title: The Cult of the Median. From the Illusion of Middle Values to the Architecture of the Real Market
detail.abstract: Percentile analytics is fundamentally incapable of describing how competition in the pay market actually works. Companies, competitors for talent, build their compensation strategies around their business model, scale, competitive position in their own product market, and pay philosophy. These practices cluster into distinct market segments that percentiles can neither detect nor describe.

title: How Strategic Crisis Team Participation Influences Middle-Line Managers’ Operational Crisis Management
affiliations: VIVE - The Danish Center for Social Science Research, VIVE - The Danish Center for Social Science Research, University of Agder and University of Agder

detail.title: How Strategic Crisis Team Participation Influences Middle-Line Managers’ Operational Crisis Management
detail.abstract: Existing research on crisis management teams (CMTs) at an organization’s strategic level has largely focused on team composition and its implications for the CMT’s decision-making processes. However, crisis decisions at the strategic level of an organization typically have an impact only when they are implemented by lower-level managers. In practice, strategic-level CMTs are typically composed of top executives, while the inclusion of lower-level managers often varies considerably. This article examines whether the CMT involvement of divisional managers influences the managers’ autonomy, their resources and upward influence, and their crisis behavior within their respective divisions. The study draws on a unique survey of local government divisional managers from the four largest Nordic countries (Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden) during COVID-19. We find that higher CMT participation is associated with divisional managers reporting greater autonomy, better access to resources, greater upward influence, and more extensive cross-organizational collaboration when conducting crisis management within their respective divisions. The results suggest that CMT composition affects not only decision-making within the CMT but also the autonomy, resources, influence and crisis behavior of managers outside the CMT.

title: How Close? Physical Distance, Tie Strength, And Network Cohesion In Dyadic Collaboration
affiliations: IESE Business School and INSEAD

detail.title: How Close? Physical Distance, Tie Strength, And Network Cohesion In Dyadic Collaboration
detail.abstract: How do social networks and physical distance jointly shape the effectiveness of interpersonal collaboration within organizations? We study how physical distance enters organizational network explanations of collaboration: It may relate to collaboration through the key components of tie strength-communication frequency and affective closeness within focal ties-while conditioning the collaborative value of network cohesion surrounding those ties. We test these arguments using longitudinal dyadic data collected before and after the relocation of two regional offices of a global pharmaceutical firm. Our baseline-adjusted models track collaborations reported at both waves and combine organizational network surveys, inter-desk walking distances, and dyadic assessments of perceived collaboration effectiveness. Monte Carlo estimates support negative indirect associations between physical distance and collaboration effectiveness through reduced communication frequency and affective closeness. The affective pathway is significantly larger; together, the two pathways account descriptively for 52.3% of the estimated association. We also find that increases in network cohesion are more strongly associated with collaboration effectiveness among dyads that moved farther apart. Incorporating physical distance therefore does not displace network explanations of collaboration; it clarifies how spatial conditions relate to collaboration, via tie strength, and when the network surrounding a collaborative relationship is most consequential.

title: Theory of European Option Underwriting Portfolios
affiliations: Heriot-Watt University

detail.title: Theory of European Option Underwriting Portfolios

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no confect of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: Writing unhedged options creates a liability-management problem in which the writer must determine both where contractual losses attach and how finite capital is distributed across those exposures. We develop a static terminal framework for European cash-settled written options that jointly represents lower put liabilities, upper call liabilities, and their capital allocations. More specifically, the model separates observed premium income from physical claim risk, expresses each liability per unit of declared capital, and evaluates the portfolio through expected underwriting surplus and the raw second moment of aggregate claims. Under a multivariate lognormal terminal law, we obtain analytical claim moments, characterize conditional capital allocation and local strike conditions, and show that Gaussian dependence affects same-tail and opposite-tail claim accumulation in different directions. We then apply the framework to archived Deribit crypto-option formations using point-in-time contract screens, fixed-moneyness benchmarks, and paired dependence-aware uncertainty. We find positive average gross-surplus differences for the staged policies in the completed samples, although the associated dispersion and tail effects are not uniform and a realized uncovered-call claim exceeds its finite capital proxy. Thus, the empirical evidence supports the use of the framework as a solvency-aware underwriting and diagnostic architecture, but it does not establish calibrated tail probabilities, executable net profitability, or broker-margin survival.

title: Before the Law takes effect: Provider Anticipatory Behavior

detail.abstract: What if the market impacts of platform regulation begin before the law actually takes effect? While traditional hierarchical firms manage regulatory compliance through top-down mandates, digital platforms face a distinct vulnerability: autonomous supply-side users can preemptively alter their operations, causing immediate platform revenue losses before a law is even enforced. This paper explores how Airbnb hosts respond during the critical approval-to-enforcement window of short-term rental regulation. Using listing-level data from five U.S. cities, combined with ordinance requirements, we show that hosts reduce supply immediately after regulatory approval, well before formal enforcement begins. The decline is gradual, grows as enforcement approaches, and reduces platform revenue and realized bookings. We argue that regulation approval itself makes future operating constraints credible, prompting hosts to reassess whether their current routines can continue under the incoming rules. To test this mechanism, we construct a Regulatory Risk Index that compares each listing's pre-approval activity to the requirements of the regulation. Listings with higher regulatory risk reduce availability more strongly, especially along the margins directly targeted by regulation, such as multi-listing operation and high prior booking intensity. These early reductions also foretell post-enforcement sorting: listings that scale back more before enforcement are less likely to apply for a license and more likely to exit. Our findings show that anticipatory behavior is not merely a threat to identification or a pre-trend to be controlled away. It is a meaningful market response through which credible future regulation begins reshaping platform supply before enforcement formally starts.

detail.abstract: Business Development Companies (BDCs) combine periodic reporting of illiquid private credit with continuously traded equity, providing a unique setting to evaluate private credit performance. During periods of credit stress, performance drops and stock-to-NAV discounts widen sharply as stock prices fall faster than reported NAVs. Market discounts and pre-announcement stock returns predict subsequent NAV markdowns and weaker profitability, although their predictive power is limited for larger BDCs and those with more diversified portfolios. Crucially, market metrics have limited ability to anticipate discrete distress events such as non-accruals and payment-in-kind (PIK) amendments. We find that quarterly NAV announcements contain significant, value-relevant incremental information that results in immediate stock price reactions.

title: The Geography of Segregation in Canada, 1891-1921

detail.title: The Geography of Segregation in Canada, 1891-1921
detail.abstract: Using full-count microdata from the Canadian census, I construct measures of residential segregation for immigrants in Canada from 1891 to 1921. I find that immigrants exhibited high segregation but also find that considerable spatial heterogeneity was also present. I then produce segregation measures for each country of origin and find that different immigrant groups experienced very different ranges of residential segregation. I illustrate the measures' value by applying them to three research questions. The results show that immigrants' segregation was pervasive in early 20th century Canada, but that its presence was also uneven across space, time, and groups.

title: Assessing the resistance of international oil trade networks to external shocks: A scenario-based graph neural network framework
affiliations: Yangtze Normal University, East China University of Science and Technology and East China University of Science and Technology - School of Business

detail.title: Assessing the resistance of international oil trade networks to external shocks: A scenario-based graph neural network framework
detail.abstract: External shocks, including geopolitical conflicts, climate-related disruptions, and public health crises, have made international oil trade networks (iOTNs) more uncertain and vulnerable. For economies on both the import and export sides, assessing structural vulnerability and adaptive capacity has become an important issue in energy trade planning and risk management. This paper develops a scenario-based graph neural network framework to evaluate shock resistance and adaptive potential in iOTNs. The framework combines graph neural networks with a heterogeneous utility function of economies to learn trade-related latent representations from annual oil trade networks, using network topology, node degree, and clustering centrality as key inputs. Guided by the learned trade-formation mechanism, negative shocks are simulated through trade-link reductions, while positive trade changes are represented by the addition of potential links under different scenario intensities. A bidirectional resistance measure is then constructed from changes in local and global centrality indicators, allowing link-loss vulnerability and trade-expansion potential to be assessed within a unified framework. The framework produces stable response patterns across different embedding dimensions and reveals clear heterogeneity in economies' attributes and network positions. At the continental level, South America, Asia, and Europe tend to remain more stable under negative shocks, whereas Oceania is more exposed to link losses and Africa shows greater potential for trade expansion. At the economy level, the United States and India are more sensitive to negative link changes, while Brazil, the Netherlands, and Canada display stronger potential for direct trade-relationship expansion under positive trade changes. The results offer quantitative evidence for identifying vulnerable economies, comparing heterogeneous network responses, and supporting vulnerability-informed planning of global oil trade systems under external disruptions.

title: Sectoral Information and the Real-Time Measurement of Trend Inflation: Evidence from Korea

detail.title: Sectoral Information and the Real-Time Measurement of Trend Inflation: Evidence from Korea

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: This research is supported by the Bank of Korea and by National Research Foundation of Korea grant No. 2018S1A5A8029423.

detail.abstract: Korea's pandemic inflation cycle-a surge that carried headline inflation to a threedecade high in 2022, a disinflation, and a renewed firming through 2026-is the country's first complete cycle since the 1990s, and it settles questions that a sample ending mid-surge cannot. We estimate trend inflation with the unobserved-components model with stochastic volatility and outliers of Stock and Watson (2016b), on headline and core inflation from 1985 and on twelve CPI sectors from 1990, extended so that the frequency of outliers is itself a time-varying state estimated by Pólya-Gamma augmentation. The surge moved the trend rather than producing a string of outliers: the twelve-sector trend rises from 1.0 percent before the pandemic to 4.8 percent in 2022, retraces about half of that, and ends at 2.6 percent with a 68-percent band above the 2-percent target; led by processed food, eating out and petroleum, it leaves an above-target trend concentrated in market services. The estimated outlier frequency has fallen by half to two-thirds since the 1990s and does not rebound, though we cannot say why: the observables usually invoked for that decline fail to explain it once they are estimated inside the model. Sectoral information also buys detection time, identifying the movement two quarters before a univariate model does under vintage-consistent seasonal adjustment, cutting real-time estimation error by more than forty percent, and delivering the lowest forecast RMSE at every horizon among the ten models compared together with the only well-calibrated predictive densities. Two properties of the estimator account for that gain: it comes from heterogeneity between the trend and the transitory loading vectors and vanishes when the two are collinear, and the seasonal-adjustment procedure enters only through the covariance of what it revises at the endpoint.

detail.abstract: We examine how decision makers adjust newsvendor ordering decisions in response to demand signals that are indicative of a demand shift. Demand shifts driven by market changes, seasonality, or external shocks create uncertainty that decision makers frequently encounter in practice. By integrating models that explain the well-known pull-to-center (PTC) effect in static newsvendor environments with models of system neglect that explain how probability judgments react to signals indicative of a demand shift, we predict when PTC and system neglect mitigate versus amplify one another. Specifically, for high-margin products in stable environments with noisy signals and low-margin products in unstable environments with precise signals, system neglect and PTC effect tend to counteract each other, resulting in ordering decisions closer to optimal levels. In the remaining profit margin and demand environments, system neglect amplifies the underordering and overordering behavior resulting from the PTC effect. We test these predictions in experimental settings with uncensored and censored demand signals and find support for our model predictions. We explore the effectiveness of decision support systems and discuss implications for providing managerial interventions in environments with salient demand shifts.

title: Care Gaps under Unequal Fiscal Capacity: Territorial Inequalities in Municipal Spending on Older People
affiliations: Ca Foscari University of Venice, Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics and Ca Foscari University of Venice

detail.title: Care Gaps under Unequal Fiscal Capacity: Territorial Inequalities in Municipal Spending on Older People

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics Research Paper Series No. 19/2026
publicationDetails.journalName: Department of Economics, Ca' Foscari University of Venice Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Population ageing is increasing pressure on local welfare systems, but the capacity of municipalities to finance and provide services for older people differs substantially across territories. This paper studies municipal expenditure on older people in Italy, focusing on the large territorial disparities observed across municipalities and regions. Using municipality-level data for 2019, before the disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the paper investigates how cross-sectional differences in per capita expenditure are associated with indicators of local needs, fiscal resources and local policy orientation. We develop a parsimonious analytical framework linking municipal expenditure to potential financial needs, local policy orientation, and fiscal resources and co-financing. Under an explicit normalization, the framework allows us to construct model-based indicators of potential financial needs and their implied coverage by predicted municipal expenditure. The results document a marked territorial divide in spending on older people and suggest that municipal expenditure covers only a limited share of estimated needs and that unequal fiscal resources contribute substantially to territorial disparities. The findings highlight the importance of local fiscal capacity and intergovernmental financing arrangements in shaping access to local services for older people across territories.

title: Management archetypes of cow–calf systems in the Espinal region of Argentina: a leverage points perspective
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Universidad de Buenos Aires, Universidad de la República, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Groningen and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Management archetypes of cow–calf systems in the Espinal region of Argentina: a leverage points perspective
detail.abstract: CONTEXT: Family-based cow-calf livestock systems in the Northern Espinal region of Argentina exhibit a gap between current and attainable performance given available resources, while the combination of management practices adopted by farmers remains poorly understood.,OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to delineate functional classes of Espinal cow-calf systems based on their strategic, tactical and monitoring or decision-support practices, and to explore how these configurations are associated with productive and environmental farm outcomes in order to suggest potential leverage points for improving system performance.,METHODS: We surveyed 55 family-based livestock farms to collect socioeconomic and management information; 30 were selected for in situ evaluation of productive and environmental indicators. Management practices were classified as strategic (long-term, system-structuring decisions), tactical (short-term adjustments), or monitoring and decision-support practices. Archetype analysis based on 14 practices was applied to 55 farms to identify extreme management configurations (archetypes) to delineate clusters around them, which were then characterized using farm-level outcomes and environmental indicators.,RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: We identified four archetypes of family livestock systems (A1–A4), differing in the number and type of practices adopted. Archetype A1, defined by a stronger orientation towards strategic management, concentrated several practices commonly associated with ecological livestock intensification. However, this configuration was not consistently associated with improved economic or environmental performance. A4 (”decision support-oriented farms”) showed a stronger emphasis on monitoring and decision support practices, such as pregnancy diagnosis, bull breeding soundness evaluation, and the use of agronomic and veterinary advice to guide management decisions. Overall, the patterns observed suggest that potential leverage points for ecological intensification may lie in the integration of strategic practices at the whole-farm level, rather than in isolated interventions.,SIGNIFICANCE: The functional classification of management practices in grass-based livestock systems of the Espinal region provides a framework for analyzing how different management configurations relate to productive and environmental outcomes. The exploratory patterns observed suggest that leverage points for ecological intensification may be more likely to emerge from system-level redesign than from the adoption of isolated practices, though this proposition requires validation with larger samples.

title: Close to Some, Distant to Others:Evaluator-Product Distance Dispersion and Polarized Reception

detail.title: Close to Some, Distant to Others:Evaluator-Product Distance Dispersion and Polarized Reception
detail.abstract: Why do some products attract both intense rejection and intense support? This paper develops and tests a relational answer: a product can be close to the prior tastes of some evaluators while being distant from the prior tastes of others. The argument separates the mean of evaluator-product distance, which shifts expected support, from the cross-evaluator spread of distance, which changes the shape of the rating distribution. A formal ordinal-threshold model shows that when latent evaluations are centered between the lowest and highest rating cutpoints, greater distance spread raises the probability mass at both endpoints and therefore increases balanced endpoint polarization. The empirical pilot uses MovieLens 100K and MovieLens 1M. Within each user, the earliest 60 percent of timestamped ratings form an 18-dimensional genre-taste profile, and the final 40 percent are held out. Audience-side distance is one minus cosine similarity between the pre-period taste profile and the focal movie vector. User and movie fixed-effect models show that a one-standard-deviation increase in distance predicts a 0.174-point rating decrease in MovieLens 100K and a 0.088-point decrease in MovieLens 1M. At the film level, a one-standard-deviation increase in the P90-P10 spread of audience distance predicts higher balanced 1-star/5-star polarization in both datasets: b = 0.00968 for 697 MovieLens 100K films and b = 0.00528 for 1,982 MovieLens 1M films. The result is deliberately narrow. Broad low-versus-high polarization and normalized variance do not replicate in MovieLens 1M, and a K = 5 community decomposition does not show that the distance spread is organized between stable taste communities. The defensible contribution is therefore a replicated association between cross-evaluator distance spread and simultaneous endpoint polarization, not a generic theory of controversy, community conflict, or causal innovation effects. A supplementary audit of a 100-indicator StarCoder transparency report is used to demonstrate claim discipline and reproducibility reporting rather than as a second test of the mechanism.

title: Optimizing Databricks Compute by Eliminating Waste, Reducing Costs, and Maximizing Performance

detail.title: Optimizing Databricks Compute by Eliminating Waste, Reducing Costs, and Maximizing Performance

detail.abstract: Cloud compute expenditure in enterprise data engineering environments is rarely the result of insufficient capacity-it is the result of insufficient governance. This paper presents a framework for Databricks compute efficiency and cost optimization grounded in policy-driven, workload-aware infrastructure management, and evaluates that framework against a structured review of publications and technical reports spanning 2020-2026, of which 23 met a source-quality screen (Section 2) and were retained. The framework specifies five operating principles-zero idle compute tolerance, workloadspecific compute selection, policy-enforced cluster configuration, serverless-first architecture, and full cost attribution-mapped onto a medallion (Bronze/Silver/Gold) reference architecture with a five-level organizational maturity model. Literature synthesis indicates partial, uneven support: among the retained studies reporting direct cost or resource-utilization reductions, figures cluster in roughly the 18-30% range, alongside improved pipeline reliability and compliance posture. We further report a twoyear, single-organization deployment case study-an anonymized enterprise finance data platform-in which application of the framework reduced steady-state monthly compute billing for the affected workload by approximately 80% (from in excess of $150,000 to approximately $30,000 per month), a larger reduction than the literaturereported range, which we attribute primarily to an unusually unmanaged starting baseline. We discuss the framework's alignment with, and points of departure from, the reviewed literature, and identify independent, multi-organization validation as the primary direction for future work.

detail.abstract: Purpose. This study examines whether the distribution of evaluations among consumers who expressed word of mouth (WOM) reflects that among users, how the gap differs across channels, and whether it arises from within-consumer selection or between-consumer differences in evaluation tendency. Design/methodology/approach. Survey data from Japanese consumers link evaluations of ten films and games to WOM through five channels: social networking sites, review sites, messaging apps, face-to-face conversation and distribution platforms. The analysis combines descriptive comparison of distributions, logit models with score-by-channel interactions, a within-between decomposition, sensitivity analyzes and counterfactual distributions. Findings. Expressed evaluation distributions departed from actual distributions in every channel and skewed toward higher evaluations, and the association between score and expression varied by channel. Contents rated relatively highly within the same consumer were more likely to be expressed in all five channels under the full coding, though not for dedicated review sites once rating-only actions are conservatively excluded; the lowevaluation within-person component was not significant. Consumers with generally high evaluation tendencies expressed WOM more often in some channels. Counterfactual comparisons substantially reduce the predicted gap, but are descriptive rather than a causal or additive decomposition. Originality. The gap is measured directly, using evaluations from consumers who expressed no WOM. Observing the same respondent-title combinations across five channels separates within-consumer selection from between-consumer composition, and shows the conclusion depends on how review activity is defined.

title: When Agents Go Viral: What OpenClaw and Moltbook Reveal About the Trillion-Dollar Trust Gap in AI
affiliations: The Digital Economist

detail.title: When Agents Go Viral: What OpenClaw and Moltbook Reveal About the Trillion-Dollar Trust Gap in AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no financial, personal, or professional relationships that could be perceived as influencing the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
This expert insights paper examines the rapid rise of autonomous AI agents through the cases of OpenClaw and Moltbook, positioning their viral adoption as a defining moment in the evolution of the agentic economy. It argues that while agents have moved beyond conversational interfaces to autonomous action—sending emails, managing transactions, coordinating schedules, and interacting across platforms—the identity, security, and trust infrastructure required to support this shift has not matured at the same pace. The result is a widening “trust gap,” where technical capability outstrips governance readiness, exposing structural vulnerabilities in how agents are verified, authorized, and supervised.

Drawing on security breakdowns, architectural comparisons, and first-hand deployment experience detailed in the paper, the analysis identifies three core fault lines: the absence of standardized digital identity for agents, the expansion of attack surfaces in high-autonomy systems, and the erosion of trust when guardrails are insufficient or misaligned with real-world risk. By contrasting open, self-governed agents with more controlled enterprise implementations, the paper demonstrates that autonomy exists along a spectrum—and that risk scales in direct proportion to delegated authority when verifiable identity, programmable constraints, and auditable records are not embedded by design.

In response, the paper introduces an “AI First, Human Always” governance framework built on seven interdependent principles: verifiable identity by default, programmable guardrails, proof of action, least privilege and lifecycle management, inclusive-by-design infrastructure, human learning autonomy, and decoupled agency with fiduciary tethering. Together, these principles form a layered governance stack intended to move organizations from experimentation toward trusted deployment at scale. Ultimately, the paper contends that the sustainability of the agentic economy will depend less on model performance and more on institutional maturity—specifically, the systems, standards, and human judgment required to ensure that autonomous agents remain accountable to the people and organizations they represent.

title: Human Identification: Solving the Cross-Industry Identity Mismatch Problem

detail.title: Human Identification: Solving the Cross-Industry Identity Mismatch Problem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed full-time in a technology role at a large U.S. financial institution not named or discussed in this paper. This paper was written independently, outside the scope of that employment, and was not commissioned, funded, reviewed, or endorsed by the author's employer. The author declares no other financial or personal relationships that could have influenced this paper's content.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper does not involve original research with human participants or patients. All industry examples (Section 4) are drawn from publicly available regulatory enforcement actions, settlement records, and previously published sources; no primary data collection, interviews, surveys, or human-subjects research were conducted.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding, grant support, or financial sponsorship from any organization. It was conducted independently by the author using publicly available sources.

detail.abstract:
Banks, hospitals, telecom providers, retailers, and government agencies each depend on the same underlying capability: matching records to a single real person. A bank reconciling a new account application, a hospital retrieving a patient's chart, a telecom provisioning a SIM, a retailer merging a loyalty profile, and a government agency verifying a benefits claim are all instances of human identification-the same problem in a different domain. In each case, an organization must resolve fragmented, inconsistent Personally Identifiable Information (PII) into a single, trustworthy representation of a real person.

When that resolution fails, the consequences are similar across sectors: duplicate records, fragmented views of the same individual, missed fraud, false compliance alerts, and eroded trust. In financial services, duplicate customer records run as high as 10–30% and have been directly implicated in regulatory penalties exceeding $3 billion (Finextra, 2024; FinCEN, 2024). In healthcare, mismatched or duplicate patient records cost the U.S. system an estimated $6.7 billion annually and account for 35% of denied claims (Imprivata; Medical Economics). In telecom and retail, poor identity resolution contributes to a broader data quality problem estimated at $3.1 trillion in annual losses across the U.S. economy, a figure originating with IBM (Redman, 2016) and still widely cited a decade later. In government, 13.2% of identity verification checks surface Social Security number mismatches, and digital identity fraud rose 33% year over year (TransUnion, 2025). 

Human identification is an industry-agnostic infrastructure problem, not a banking specific or healthcare specific one — solving it well means building for every industry, not just one. Today’s dominant approaches — deterministic rule  based matching and probabilistic scoring — increasingly fall short as data volume, fragmentation, and privacy regulation grow. This paper proposes a vendor neutral reference architecture: an AI-powered entity resolution capability combining graph based relationship modeling, machine learned probabilistic matching, and persistent “golden record” identifiers. Organizations that have adopted this approach report 80–90% reductions in duplicate records and 40–60% reductions in false positive compliance or fraud alerts (Winpure, 2024; Quantexa, 2024), outcomes documented across financial services, healthcare, telecommunications, retail, and government.

title: Navigating B2B SaaS Adoption in Emerging Markets: Field Research on Clinical UI/UX, Regulatory Frictions, and Trust Networks in the Uzbekistan Dental Sector

detail.title: Navigating B2B SaaS Adoption in Emerging Markets: Field Research on Clinical UI/UX, Regulatory Frictions, and Trust Networks in the Uzbekistan Dental Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and developer of Denapp, the B2B SaaS platform analyzed in this research. No other financial or personal relationships influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Field observations and beta evaluations were conducted with signed informed consent from participating clinic administrators and practitioners. Individual patient records were anonymized to ensure data privacy.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was independently conducted.

detail.abstract: Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) frameworks optimized for developed Western markets frequently encounter extreme churn and near-zero adoption when deployed directly into emerging market micro-enterprises. This paper investigates the structural, economic, and human-computer interaction (HCI) barriers to software adoption within the private dental clinical sector of Tashkent Region, Uzbekistan. Drawing upon qualitative field observations and founder research-including early market sales attempts, 10 cold physical clinic pitches across Akhangaran, and a multi-month beta deployment across 3 private clinics involving 20 active practitioners and 3,000+ unique patient records-we evaluate how non-price frictions impact technology integration. Our findings demonstrate that clinical software adoption relies on three critical pillars: (1) cognitive noise reduction and zero-training affordance design (demonstrated by optimizing patient Telegram authentication from 8 steps down to 1 QR scan and replacing rigid diagnostic requirements with flexible multi-teeth action workflows), (2) compliance with mandatory national digital health infrastructures (such as Uzbekistan's DMED regulatory framework), and (3) navigating localized, non-monetary trust networks (e.g., informal choyxona referrals and regional barter/debt dynamics). We synthesize these observations into a six-rule practical framework for B2B SaaS development in transition economies.

title: Close to Some, Distant to OthersEvaluator-Product Distance Dispersion and Polarized Reception

detail.title: Close to Some, Distant to OthersEvaluator-Product Distance Dispersion and Polarized Reception
detail.abstract: Why do some products attract both intense rejection and intense support? This paper develops and tests a relational answer: a product can be close to the prior tastes of some evaluators while being distant from the prior tastes of others. The argument separates the mean of evaluator-product distance, which shifts expected support, from the cross-evaluator spread of distance, which changes the shape of the rating distribution. A formal ordinal-threshold model shows that when latent evaluations are centered between the lowest and highest rating cutpoints, greater distance spread raises the probability mass at both endpoints and therefore increases balanced endpoint polarization. The empirical pilot uses MovieLens 100K and MovieLens 1M. Within each user, the earliest 60 percent of timestamped ratings form an 18-dimensional genre-taste profile, and the final 40 percent are held out. Audience-side distance is one minus cosine similarity between the pre-period taste profile and the focal movie vector. User and movie fixed-effect models show that a one-standard-deviation increase in distance predicts a 0.174-point rating decrease in MovieLens 100K and a 0.088-point decrease in MovieLens 1M. At the film level, a one-standard-deviation increase in the P90-P10 spread of audience distance predicts higher balanced 1-star/5-star polarization in both datasets: b = 0.00968 for 697 MovieLens 100K films and b = 0.00528 for 1,982 MovieLens 1M films. The result is deliberately narrow. Broad low-versus-high polarization and normalized variance do not replicate in MovieLens 1M, and a K = 5 community decomposition does not show that the distance spread is organized between stable taste communities. The defensible contribution is therefore a replicated association between cross-evaluator distance spread and simultaneous endpoint polarization, not a generic theory of controversy, community conflict, or causal innovation effects. A supplementary audit of a 100-indicator StarCoder transparency report is used to demonstrate claim discipline and reproducibility reporting rather than as a second test of the mechanism.

title: A hybrid GARCH-LSTM model for Chinese carbon market volatility forecasting
affiliations: Xuzhou University of Technology, Xuzhou University of Technology, Xuzhou University of Technology, Xuzhou University of Technology and Huaibei Normal University

detail.title: A hybrid GARCH-LSTM model for Chinese carbon market volatility forecasting

keywords.keywords: Hybrid GARCH-LSTM model；Chinese carbon market；Volatility forecasting；Discontinuous trading

detail.abstract: Accurate forecasting of carbon market price volatility is of significant importance. The Chinese carbon market primarily relies on daily data, characterized by short time series and discontinuous trading, posing substantial challenges for volatility prediction. Constructing an integrated model that combines econometric models with deep learning is crucial for addressing the issues of long memory and structural breakpoints in carbon financial markets. This paper develops a comprehensive hybrid forecasting model that integrates the Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) family models with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) artificial neural networks, consisting of three stages. In the first stage, based on the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), all historical information up to time t is selected to estimate the benchmark GARCH model in a rolling-window fashion. In the second stage, the updated conditional volatility and standardized return series are used to construct a feature matrix incorporating multi-source information. In the third stage, this feature matrix is input into a pre-trained and fixed-parameter LSTM model to obtain the volatility forecast for time t+1. The empirical results demonstrate that compared to traditional GARCH volatility forecasting models, the prediction accuracy of the proposed method is significantly improved.

title: Developing a TISM Model of Consumer Awareness in E-Pharmacy Adoption: A Qualitative Study Approach
affiliations: COER University and Andhra University

detail.title: Developing a TISM Model of Consumer Awareness in E-Pharmacy Adoption: A Qualitative Study Approach
detail.abstract: The Rapid expansion of e-pharmacy services has transformed access to medicines by enabling consumers to obtain pharmaceutical products remotely, thereby improving convenience and accessibility. However, consumer awareness and informed adoption of e-pharmacy services remain influenced by multiple technological, economic, logistical, regulatory, informational, and trust-related considerations. Despite the growing relevance of e-pharmacy in India, limited qualitative research has systematically examined the factors shaping consumer awareness of its adoption. This study, therefore, aims to explore and develop an empirically grounded framework of the factors influencing consumer awareness of e-pharmacy adoption in the Indian context. Grounded Theory Methodology (GTM) was employed to generate insights from in-depth interviews with 13 domain experts. Through systematic qualitative analysis, ten categories influencing consumer awareness were identified: convenience and accessibility; prescription management; regulatory and legal uncertainties; lack of internet access; data security and privacy; information literacy; and word-of-mouth influence. Collectively, these categories indicate that e-pharmacy awareness is not determined solely by technological convenience but emerges from the interaction of accessibility, affordability, service reliability, regulatory assurance, information capabilities, privacy and security, and interpersonal influence. The study contributes to the emerging e-pharmacy literature by developing a contextually grounded framework for understanding the determinants of consumer awareness in India. The findings also have practical implications for e-pharmacy providers, pharmacists, policymakers, and other healthcare stakeholders in designing strategies to enhance consumer awareness, trust, responsible medicine use, and informed adoption of digital pharmacy services.

title: Development of an Integrated Construction Safety Leadership (ICSL) Model and Its Implications for the Australian Construction Industry
affiliations: University of Newcastle, University of Newcastle, University of Newcastle, University of Newcastle and University of Newcastle

detail.title: Development of an Integrated Construction Safety Leadership (ICSL) Model and Its Implications for the Australian Construction Industry
detail.abstract: The construction industry is constantly seeking effective safety leadership styles, a task complicated by several inherent factors, including the project-based nature, high labour turnover, intricate subcontracting chains, production pressure, and emerging psychosocial hazards. Addressing complexities requires hybrid, integrated approaches that leverage Behaviour-Based Safety (BBS), transactional leadership, and transformational leadership. To meet this challenge, the present study introduces the Integrated Construction Safety Leadership (ICSL) framework: a novel, theory-informed model to enable safer, more diverse, and adaptive leadership in complex construction environments. This method follows Design-based Research (DBR) and is informed by principles of systems thinking, resilience engineering, psychosocial safety climate theory, and Safety-II theories. ICSL incorporates eight key elements: multi-level integration, systems thinking, cultural infrastructure, fair accountability, WHS alignment, operational flexibility, psychological safety, and evidence-informed adaptation. It is conceptually aligned with the Work Health and Safety (WHS) Act (2011), ISO 45003, and the industry call for innovation through both Safety Differently and learning teams. This article provides a critical review of current leadership models, outlines the theoretical development of ICSL, and explains how to contextualise it within the Australian construction industry. ICSL is scalable across contractor tiers and works in both tier-one and SME environments. The research concludes by highlighting the framework's theoretical contributions, its significance for legal and practical aspects, and its implications for future empirical research. ICSL offers a significant pathway for regulators, researchers, and industry leaders to reimagine safety leadership as a practice that is culturally responsive, psychologically safe, and operationally viable in the evolving, high-hazard construction environment.
